speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to use my allotted ten minutes to make a few brief comments on this legislation which will restrict the indexing of basic pensions of senior Canadians.

As Members are well aware, this Bill is only one of a number of measures designed to encourage all Canadians to lower their expectations. Although limited indexation of the basic old age pension for those who do not need the supplement will generate estimated after-tax program savings of $49 million in 1983 and 1984, the purpose of this Bill is not to save money, as I have often explained.
Members opposite, by the way, will notice that that sum of money totalling $49 million is drastically lower than the earlier estimated savings of $84 million, and I am very pleased about that. This is a clear indication that the inflation rate is being brought down in Canada. I say that because the New Democratic Party does not seem to be aware of this fact. In every speech made by NDP Members they continue to quote figures which are now seven months old. This is a very dangerous and misleading practice, and I would just ask them to be honest with Canadians, particularly senior Canadians.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said in Toronto last week, the Consumer Price Index dropped from an annual rate of 11.5 per cent in the second quarter of 1982 to 9.7 per cent in the fourth quarter, which is excellent.

February 3, 1983
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
The Elon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) said that seniors were losing something like $300. I would like to make it clear that that is total misinformation. I want to repeat that all senior citizens who have no or little income apart from their basic pension will not be affected by this Bill. I also want to say to those seniors who will be affected by this Bill in small amounts that we will not be collecting back any money on the January cheque which was fully indexed. We will not collect back any money.
Hon. Members opposite have attempted to make Canadians believe that these measures are dismantling the improvements that have been made through the decades to the pension system. That is not true. These charges are false. What is worse, they serve only to create unwarranted anxiety among the elderly.
We know the political game played in this Chamber by every Member in the two Opposition Parties, who always accuse us of being terrible villains. That is the game played in the House. But, when those Members go outside and, instead of quoting figures of $18 in total loss for this year and $39 for next year, they quote figures like $300, they are not damaging us, since we were elected by a majority and we will pass this Bill. They are damaging Mrs. X and Mr. Y, who are at home watching on TV and do not know the real figures. They suddenly become nervous about losing $300. That figure is false. This Bill does not do that at all.
I would like to reply to Members who think that we are doing terrible things to the pension system. I say to those Hon. Members and all Canadians that I am very proud that we have kept the social programs the way they are. Last week, we all watched television when President Reagan delivered a State of the Union message in which he outlined a four-part plan to increase growth and reduce deficits. Who is going to pay the bill? He cited what he termed the need to reduce, and I quote, "the dangerous growth rate in government spending". Where did he find the money? He called for a six-month freeze in the cost of living adjustment-that means zero growth-for government-related pension programs. He spoke of cutting back on food stamps and other such social programs. In addition, he proposed asking the elderly to pay more for medicare.
The United States is not alone in doing that to social programs. In West Germany, Chancellor Helmut Kohl has proposed to delay statutory cost of living increases in old age pensions due in January until July, at which time pensioners will also be required to pay health insurance contributions.
I could go on and on giving examples of other measures that have taken place. In France, for example, people will have to pay for medicare.

decided on their social programs. Mr. Speaker, members opposite say to the Canadian people that we are dismantling the social programs. I am proving the contrary to them with facts-they never like to hear facts-and with quotations on things that can be verified about what is happening elsewhere.
We are not dismantling the program in Canada; we are making sure that seniors get the full value of their dollar in their pension. We are doing that by a national campaign of 6 and 5 per cent, which is working. That is why Hon. Members opposite are so furious and the proof of that is in many of their speeches. They ask, "If it is such a success, why do it?" Well, Mr. Speaker, if we do not do it, it will stop being a success. Members do not seem to realize the psychological dimension of the economic cycle.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that social welfare spending is under attack in most countries of the western world. But this country has respected its basic commitments and pensioners will not be subjected to the sorts of draconian measures that the elderly in many other countries are now facing. Bill C-131 safeguards the principles of both universality and indexation.
Despite the laughter from the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to finish my remarks by inviting all Hon. Members to support the bill. The faster we reduce inflation, the sooner all Canadians, especially pensioners, those on fixed incomes, will benefit.

inflation which, as you know, would have been an 11.5 per cent raise. How does the Minister plan to get around the position where you are better off with a smaller pension from the Canada Pension Plan than a larger one?

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
There are times, Mr. Speaker, in this House, when we should attempt to use the medium of television and radio to speak to the nation. There are other times when we should try to direct our attention to the Hon. Members of this House, because it is only the Hon. Members of this House who can do something about a tragic wrong which is about to be perpetrated on some Canadians. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is that kind of a day.
At six o'clock this evening, Hon. Members of this House will be forced to stand and vote. The Minister is asking Hon. Members of the Liberal Party to stand in this House and impose a special lifetime tax on every Canadian who is 65 years of age and over. It is a lifetime tax which has an immediate consequence in the year 1983. It is a tax which will grow in size and consequence in every succeeding year. In this time of economic difficulty, with budget deficits running in the order of $24 billion, she is asking a particular sub-group, one which represents the poorest segment of Canadian society, to bear a tax, a minimum 3 per cent special tax which no one else would pay, which would last a lifetime and which would grow.
In this Chamber, at six o'clock this evening, we can put a stop to that. Before my remarks are concluded, I will move a motion which will delay debate and thus leave the current law in place. Anyone on the Liberal side who has a social conscience and supports that motion will be ensuring that this special tax is not imposed on senior citizens, those who are 65 years of age and over.
Why in the name of justice, in the name of humanity, is Party discipline about to prevail on an issue which is so ill-considered and so unnecessary? The Minister told us this morning that she estimates the savings to the federal treasury this year to be $18 million. That amounts to 15 cents per month per taxpayer. If every taxpayer in this country was willing to donate 1 5 cents per month, this piece of legislation would not be necessary.
There have been estimates that this Chamber costs something in the order of half a million dollars a day to operate. We will have taken the time of this Chamber for approximately six days on this piece of legislation. We will have cost the Canadian taxpayers at least $3 million to debate this Bill which is intended to save the Government $18 million and make the lives of every senior citizen who lives at or near an income level of $9,000 a year poorer. The Bill would impose a very special tax on senior citizens who make $750 a month, who must provide themselves with shelter, transportation, recreation, food and medicine. They earn $750 a month, and there are many of them, and they are being asked to absorb a special 3 per cent to 5 per cent tax this year which will be in the order of 4 per cent next year and 5 per cent the year after, because it multiplies in that fashion. I ask, where is the sanity in the Cabinet? Where is the social conscience of Members of Parliament who have been sent here by their constituents?
I have absolutely no doubt that if the Government were to ask every single Canadian taxpayer, ten million people who pay taxes, if they were willing to contribute 15 cents a month more in taxes so that the senior citizens of this country would not have to pay a special tax and the Government would not have to take money out of their pockets, 99.9 per cent of the time the answer would be, "Yes, I will pay the extra 15 cents a month".
February 3, 1983

Why can we not have a Government that thinks about the trade-off? Why can we not have a Government which says that if Canadians are willing to pay 15 cents a month, it can treat our senior citizens better, with dignity, give them an opportunity to eat more nutritious meals and enable them to survive without the fear and threat which this piece of legislation represents?
The Government will tell us that it had to do this to bring down inflation. That argument is not credible. To believe that, in an economy which operates in the order of $300 billion, the sum of $18 million is a significant factor in inflation is nonsense. There is no inflationary reason for this piece of legislation. It is incredible.
Then the Government says: "But we will increase the Guaranteed Income Supplement"; and yes, it will. Every senior citizen who makes less than $750 a month will keep the income he would have received without this Bill. If one makes less than $750 a month, the Government, the Liberal Party, will not take any money away if one is over 65 years of age. However, if one makes $750 a month or $755 or $760, the Government will put a special tax on one's income.
In December we were told in committee that the tax was about 5 per cent. Today the Minister stood up and told us that it is about 3 per cent. It does not even matter if it is three-tenths of 1 per cent, the principle is wrong. People over the age of 65 are the people who created the wealth in this country. They include homesteaders who took down the trees and plowed the fields for the first time. They include miners who dug the first mines and built the first shafts. They include carpenters and plumbers who are busy and have been teaching younger people their skills. This is part of our population to which all of us who are younger owe the most. Without their contribution to this nation, we would not have an economy with the wealth to distribute.
It is simply inconceivable that Hon. Members opposite, like a bunch of sheep, will stand up later this day and impose a special tax on people over 65. It is a logic which says, "Let us identify the poorest segment of the Canadian population and make them pay a tax which no other part of the population must pay". The Government does not say to someone who is 21, 22 or 40 years of age that he or she cannot go out and work double time or work at a little part-time job to augment one's income. However, in the Government's social policy system, it says to the senior citizens: "You have Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement. If you make more than $750 a month, we will take part of it away from you in this special fashion. If you go out and earn some more, you must tell us about it and we will take some more public money away from you."
If we had sat down, Mr. Speaker, to design a combination of social programs and legislation which would have a maximum negative impact on a particular part of the population, it would
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
be this legislation. These people are less able to help themselves in an economic sense. The vast majority of them are out of the labour force and are dependent on those assets built up throughout a lifetime of participation in the labour force. As they planned their retirement, one of those assets which they counted on was the fact that they would get an Old Age Security cheque indexed so that it would grow if there was inflation. They had a commitment from the Canadian people, through the Parliament of Canada, that they could prepare their retirement plans in the belief that coming generations would keep that commitment. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we cannot stand in this Chamber later this day and break that commitment. It is inhuman and insane, and there are other options.
The option I laid out today, Mr. Speaker, is 15 cents per month from every taxpayer and we do not have to pass this legislation. Canadians would gladly give that 15 cents, I am sure of it. I see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) in the House. I have raised the issue of the buying out of public funds of some $650 million worth of service stations. The Government does that, and then turns around in the House of Commons and says we can afford that expenditure but we cannot give $18 million to senior citizens.
I have on my desk a report from Ultramar Canada Limited which concludes that the taxpayers of this country are spending $517 million this year just on the financing for Petro-Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am going to go out in the next federal election and tell the Canadian people, in the best way I am able to and on every platform I can get, that every elected Member of the Liberal Party in this House in the year 1983 stood up and said a subsidy of $517 million to Petro-Canada and the purchase of $650 million worth of service stations is more important and a priority, and therefore we have to cut pensions. We have to impose a tax on senior citizens this year, next year and every other year of their lives. Cut out the bafflegab, cut through the legislation, and that is the nub of it. It is not right, it dishonours this Chamber and it dishonours our commitment and those people and their lifetime of commitment to this nation. And we have six more hours to decide not to do it.
If Members opposite stand in this Chamber at six o'clock tonight and vote for this Bill, then it is done; they have broken that commitment. I say to whoever is listening on the television network: "Regardless whether you are over 65 or under 65, find out who your Member of Parliament is, find out how he votes later this day, and if you do not like it, you can do something about it. You can join a political party that is different from the one that Member represents in this Chamber"-and I suspect in most cases it will be a Liberal-"and you can have power in this nation. You can work as a volunteer to make sure that any Member who does this, whose social conscience is so weak and so ill considered, never has an opportunity to sit in this Chamber again." It takes volunteers and commitment but it can be done, and if people out therein

February 3, 1983

television land are as mad as I am, then it will be a ground-swell which will sweep this Government away and things will change with a new Parliament.
When we come back here we will honour the commitment. Members of this Party will first of all honour the commitment to provide a healthy economy, one that produces wealth so that we can keep our commitment to the senior citizens of this country and those who are not able to take care of themselves.
I implore, Mr. Speaker, I beg Members of the Liberal Party of Canada who sit in this Chamber to support my motion. It does not bring down the Government and cause an election; all it does is stop this legislation so senior citizens in this country will get the pension they are entitled to. It is wrong to impose a special and abusive tax on the poorest segment of the Canadian population. It is wrong, wrong, wrong.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to move the following motion:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor: "Bill C-131, An Act to amend the Old Age Security Act (No. 2), be not now read a third time but that it be read a third time this day six months hence."
Please, let us do what is right for the senior citizens of this nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I rise to oppose strongly Bill C-131 because of its impact on senior citizens across the land and also because of the principle it represents; that is the erosion of universal social programs in Canada. This is something which we believe is a basic right of all Canadians.
This is the third time many of my colleagues and I have risen to speak against the Bill. We feel very strongly that no protest can be too great. Although perhaps we in the NDP are few in number, we feel so strongly about this matter that we want to keep the opposition to this Bill going for as long as

February 3, 1983
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
possible. We appeal to our colleagues on the right to continue this protest. We regret that they did not have the same kind of sympathy for workers, as my colleague just said, in relation to opposing Bill C-124.
I spoke on December 2 about the impact of Bill C-131 on older women. This is of particular concern to me and to my colleagues. The New Democratic Party has been involved in a major task force concerning older women. We have travelled to every Province, to the Yukon and to the Territories. The same story has been told to us over and over again. Older women in Canada not only had very low wages if they worked, but by far the majority of them who now are pensioners received no wages at all because they were home makers. They were the ones who worked hard raising families. They had no pay and now they have no benefits. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) knows this only too well. I have heard her express her concern for this group of Canadians. This Bill is completely contradictory to any concern the Minister once had for older women in particular.
I spoke on December 21 about the impact of this Bill on ordinary people. At that time I tried to get as many figures as 1 could from British Columbia where the cost of living has been excessively high. I took a look at my own riding of Vancouver East. There are many retired people from immigrant families and working class families whose wages were low. There are very many people who have been poor most of their lives; many of them were on welfare and again a great many of these are women.
Today I would like to summarize our concerns once more and appeal to the Government in the last stage to throw out this Bill. I want to appeal to the Liberals in the name of justice. We do not want to treat this matter as our friends to the right are treating it. They are treating it as a humanitarian concern, that we should be good to our old folks. That is patronizing and condescending. This is a matter of basic justice for Canadians.
Pensioners who have worked all their lives should not have to bear the brunt of restraint. They did not cause this country's inflation. Most of them will recognize that the Liberal Government that is bringing this in also is responsible for doing very little to control inflation in Canada. Pensioners are the victims of inflation. They are the ones who go to the grocery store and see the prices rising every month. They cannot buy meat very often for their diets. They are finding it hard to find enough money for fresh vegetables. If they live in rental accommodation, their rents are excessively high. If they are lucky enough to be in senior citizens' residences-and heaven knows, there are not enough of them-they still have to consider escalating costs of telephone, utilities and transportation. Very few of them have money to get out and just be a part of society. Those who have their own homes have been faced with high increases in taxes. There is no extra money in senior citizens' budgets these days except those of the very wealthy.
I appeal to the Government, not only from the basic justice point of view, which the Government owes to elderly Canadians, but also on the basis of need. I am not just talking about those Canadians with the lowest income who qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement; they are far below the poverty level and, of course, the cost of living hits them the hardest. I am talking also about the middle group, some 100,000 Canadian pensioners whose total income for a year is little more than S6,000. They are not eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, but now they are faced with having the cost of living index capped at half what it should be. It is that group which this Bill will affect the most. Surely any Member who knows his or her constituents must have talked to senior citizens. Surely Members have gone to the supermarkets and have watched how the seniors have to scrimp and save, how bare their baskets are as they go through the cash registry with very little. Surely most Members of Parliament know there is a great need for pensioners to have full indexing.
I want to repeat what I said the last time I spoke to the House on this Bill about the Bill's impact on women. This bill is unfair to elderly women who make up over 50 per cent of our old age pensioners. By far the greatest proportion of elderly women live below the poverty level. We have lots of statistics to prove this point. They are poor, and because they are poor, they usually are alone and isolated in rooms, in apartments and sometimes even in their own family home. Few people go to see them and they have no money to get out and be a part of society. They suffer discrimination not only because they are old but also because they are women. Most of them do not have the Canada Pension Plan, nor do they have coverage from private pensions. Those who are married live longer than their husbands. Many of them, if not most of them over the age of 65, are alone and have only one old age pension with which to pay all the costs of living. It is much easier for two people to stretch the pension cheque.
We believe this Bill is particularly unfair to older women. Most older women are in this marginal group, not poor enough in Government terms, to have GIS, but, God knows, in reality they are poor, and they do not have enough income to cover their cost of living.
What are we doing if this Bill passes, which it will because of the Liberal majority? We are telling the older pensioners, most of whom are women, that they do not deserve full indexing, even though it had been promised them in past legislation.
I appeal to the Government to reconsider this Bill in its last stages. It dishonours elderly people: we have heard other Members say that. We are so proud of the older people who have given so much to Canada. We all know families-our own families, friends' families, and so on-who have had members go through two wars and have lost members of their family. All of them have suffered the struggles of life during the depression. They gave up full indexing during the depression. They did not have enough to live on in those days. They cut their costs and they made over old clothes. They struggled
February 3, 1983

to raise families. They should not have to be faced with this situation now they are in their later years.
As we have all said, our senior citizens are the people who have contributed their labour to Canada. They own a share of the resources of this country. They raised families. They contributed leadership. They deserve a full pension with full indexing.
I would like to remind the Government that we oppose this Bill because it does not make financial sense. It takes away close to $400 from senior citizens because their pensions are being reduced, but it will do nothing to create jobs. I think the net saving is about $84 million, a very minimal amount of money when you consider how other expenditures are being allocated in our federal budget, Mr. Speaker. Dome alone was given $500 million. There are many other expenditures which could have been cut that would have created much less hardship for the people who are the victims of inflation and who are now being made the victims of the Government's restraint program.
Finally, we oppose this Bill because we strongly believe, as do many of the groups who presented briefs to the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, that the Bill represents a means of eroding the universality of social programs. In this case, it is old age pensions. We believe this to be the case no matter how strongly the Minister denies it. This is a regressive measure.
We know that the Liberal Cabinet, the Minister of Finance in particular, tried very hard last summer to do away with universal old age pensions and Family Allowances. I would remind those Hon. Members opposite that it was Liberals across the country who protested very strongly against the erosion of universality.
We believe that fully indexed pensions are a right. If indexing is removed, the universal concept of old age pensions is removed. It represents the erosion of a basic social program and right which this Party fought so very hard to introduce. We will fight just as hard to oppose a reduction in indexation. Pensions must be indexed to the real cost of living.
The Conservatives have been very hypocritical if one recalls what they said about reductions to workers' wages. If they feel strongly about this Bill, let them relinquish part of their wages to back up one of their arguments for Bill C-124, for example.
We believe that this Bill represents bad politics. As I have said, Liberal supporters across the country have gone on record as saying that they want universality and fully protected pensions and Family Allowances. We disagree with this Bill in principle, but may I remind Liberal Members that pensioners are voters. We are not opposing this Bill simply to be pragmatic and solicit votes, but let the pragmatic Liberals remember that many voters are pensioners. We will do our best to remind those pensioners in two years, or when the next election comes about, that it was the Liberals who cut back old age pensions. Undoubtedly, the Government will offer something to the
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
pensioners to gain their vote shortly before the election but the pensioners will remember and will be reminded that they cannot be used as symbols in a restraint program or flattered with pre-election goodies.
In the time I have remaining I would like to refer to briefs that were presented by a number of organizations to the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs during its debate on this Bill. Time only permits a brief excerpt from these presentations but it is important to put them on the record. I would urge those who are concerned about this Bill not just to take the word of the NDP but also to consider the views of many credible organizations that have experience in social policies. These groups include pensioners' organizations who are certainly experts on the question of pensions and the needs of the elderly in Canada, as well as groups that represent Canadian women.
I would first like to refer to a brief from the National Council on Welfare dated July, 1982:
Many elderly men and women who live at or just above the poverty line will be hurt by the Government's restraint program. A single pensioner with a total income of as low as $9,200-more than $500 below the poverty line for large urban centres-will sacrifice about $55, just the same as someone living on affluent income.
In other words, those who earn high incomes will receive the same cut in indexing as those with marginal incomes. The brief went on to say that over 100,000 poor and near poor elderly Canadians will suffer.
On December 9, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women said that they-
-condemned the federal Government for limiting the cost of living indexation of Family Allowances and old age pensions. The two Liberal ceilings on indexation Bills do not improve the system but simply try to take advantage of the vulnerability of women and old people. Those most affected by Bill C-131 are the near poor elderly whose income is just a little too high to entitle them to the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women said on December 13:
Women are facing a reduction of 3 per cent to 5 per cent in the real value of Family Allowance and pensions. It is difficult to understand how indexing pensions below the level of need meets the objectives of the green paper on pension reform, which states that elderly Canadians should be guaranteed a minimum level of income. The recent Report of the Auditor General suggests that there may be other means of reducing Government spending.
We know what those means are. They would certainly be a higher restraint priority in the opinion of our Party.
On December 14 the Canadian Labour Council said:
Bill C-131 is extremely unjust because it is a tax that falls solely on people over 65, most of whom are people of modest means. Nothing is being said about tax exemptions for the elderly which actually provide benefits that increase with the taxable income-
The National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation felt that there should be full indexing and pensions above the poverty line.
The Canadian Council on Retirees strongly object to restraint programs which force pensioners to give up part of their pension increase and strongly oppose the attack on universality.

February 3, 1983
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
All of these organizations and many more have said that this Bill is poor, unjust and denies the promises that were made to senior citizens in pension policies that were adopted by the Liberal Government and the House of Commons. Those policies provided that there must be full indexing. This Bill is in conflict with those policies. Senior citizens in Canada today suffer the most from the high cost of living.
Bill C-131 is particularly hard on women pensioners who are very poor. Many of them have lived on one pension for many years and are trying to stretch their earnings to meet the cost of living.
This Bill erodes the whole concept of universality. I would urge the Minister to reflect upon her statements during the last days of debate on this Bill and to try to live up to her reputation, which I am afraid she is losing, of being concerned about elderly Canadians and women. Of course, we will continue to oppose Bill C-131 as long as we can, for all the reasons I have mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, 1 heard the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) say that the Conservatives were fighting this Bill on some kind of compassionate grounds, as if we had to be nice to the old folks-1 believe those were her words. I want to tell the Hon. Member that 1 am participating in this debate, as so many of my colleagues are, out of a sense of outrage over the injustice that is being perpetrated against senior citizens, not out of any misplaced sense of compassion or something left over from Sunday morning.
I say that the Government is playing with a type of economic yo-yo, using the senior citizens of our country. When the Liberals spin the wheel and want a little bit of political popularity coming into the election, they will promise senior citizens something; but when they spin the wheel again and ask where they can find a few bucks-in this case, a few lousy bucks, given the outrageous expenses of the federal Government and the $23 billion deficit-their first targets are senior citizens, who are vulnerable and defenceless except for the people in the House who stand and fight this type of outrageous legislation from the viewpoint of injustice, not simply compassion.
I want the Hon. Member for Vancouver East to hear me on this matter. I feel just as strongly about the outrage over the problems facing women, especially those over the age of 65. 1 have gone door-to-door through Edmonton South, supposedly one of the better areas of Canada, but where all kinds of senior citizens, particularly women, are living just inside the margin of poverty. That is just an absolute outrage and a scandal. It is also a scandal that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), with whom we are trying to communicate in this debate, does not even take the courtesy to listen to what is being said.
I wonder what is the real purpose of Parliament, the purpose of debate and the purpose of the new rules. It was really
amazing to me that when the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) proposed an amendment that this Bill be hoisted for six months, setting out his very serious argument, it was as though it was sort of pro forma. We are trying to communicate to the people of Canada that this Party deeply cares about senior citizens, and we want this injustice which is being perpetrated against them to be given six months' study. What is unreasonable about that?
I fully support the Hon. Member in his challenge to see, at six o'clock tonight, how many Hon. Members opposite feel that an injustice is being perpetrated on our senior citizens, who are being asked to carry an unfair burden in the fight against inflation.
I want to deal with some of the arguments put forward by the Minister. I believe she has not really challenged our fundamental objections to Bill C-131. I even wonder how much heart she has herself in carrying forward the Government's intention of pushing this Bill through by the unholy use of closure once again. It is not good enough that the Liberals will not accept more time for study; they cut off debate in the House of Commons when Hon. Members are trying to speak for those of our citizens who need us the most. It is an absolute outrage. They are breaking a commitment to the senior citizens of this country. The Government has not justified the real hardship-

speechtext:
I am certainly pleased that the NDP will support this amendment. I wish on other occasions, when there were votes of critical importance to the future of this country, that the NDP had taken such an attitude of support for solid principles of legislation. I have certain memorable votes of the NDP in mind when I make that comment.
The problem which this Bill poses for the principle of universality and social security has not yet been addressed. When weighed against the fundamental concerns now being presented by myself and my Party, one finds that the Government has only offered, once again, the hollow plea of six and five and has even been unable to give evidence that there will be substantive savings in Government expenditure should the Bill pass.
My most important objection to Bill C-131 is that it breaks an undertaking given to citizens of Canada, in this case the
February 3, 1983

segment of the population which is the most vulnerable. It is certainly not a matter of violating a written agreement, as was the case with Public Service pensions in Bill C-133. In this case it is a question of reneging on a social contract. The Minister of National Health and Welfare herself made this point when she opened the debate on the Bill. At that time she said:
There is a social contract, as it were, that guarantees a basic pension for everyone.
I also cited the Minister in my remarks two days ago. She said that the Government "had no intention of changing the rules of the game", and that it would "maintain indexing of the Old Age Security pension". As late as November 4, the Minister claimed:
All social programs, that means in particular pensions and benefits for children, will remain as they are.
Why? The Minister then reassured:
People are in the middle of an economic crisis and they need stability.
Breaking a trust and taking money from people's pockets certainly does not promote this stability to which the Minister paid lip service. On this theme, I wish to quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Speaking last April at the National Pension Conference, he stated:
Put simply, people must be protected in their retirement years. The Canadian Government has pledged that they will be better protected in the future than they are now. Pensions which are not protected against inflation naturally tend to dwindle over the years. People who thought they had purchased protection for the rest of their lives find they face more serious financial problems the older they become.
I ask Your Honour, in view of this Bill, which is hurtling through its final hours in the House, how are the senior citizens of this country to have faith in the Prime Minister's word?
What is doubly galling is the fact that in so breaking its obligations to the elderly of this country, the Government would somehow like us to believe that its actions are not arbitrary, not unilateral. Again citing the Minister of National Health and Welfare, her Government is "asking 1.1 million pensioners to help lead the way in the fight against inflation". She asserted that she was "very conscious of the sacrifice we are asking", to use the Minister's words.
It is preposterous to suggest that pensioners have, in any way, shape or form, been "asked", for Bill C-131 dictates to the elderly that Old Age Security is no longer inflation-proof. As if that were not bad enough, the Government rams closure through the House in order to get the Bill passed. It is fortunate that the Government agreed to spare the poorest of pensioners this decrease in indexation by making up the loss in Old Age Security benefits through the annual Guaranteed Income Supplement, which continues, thankfully, to rise with the cost of living. However, by placing greater emphasis on the income-tested GIS, this measure threatens the cardinal principle of universality. To a greater extent, the elderly will be burdened with the welfare stigma associated with GIS, playing down the universality of OAS or a Government pension as a right. This manoeuvre, moreover, would seem to
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
increase the administrative complexity of the entire pension question.
My next major point concerns the hardship which Bill C-131 would create for the 1.1 million pensioners who are not covered by the Guaranteed Income Supplement. Estimates are that this Bill will cost them approximately $290 each over 1983 and 1984, or about $12 a month. According to the National Council on Welfare, about 100,000 pensioners are classified as poor or near poor among these 1.1 million, those single recipients of Old Age Security with incomes between $9,000 and $10,000 annually who do not qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement; or, similarly, couples with incomes of $15,000 or $16,000 who are not receiving the GIS.
The Government is fighting inflation on the backs of those who can least afford it. It is singling out the elderly in an effort to extricate itself from the problems caused by its own economic mismanagement. The Bill cuts back on the Government's moral obligation to aid senior citizens. They have left the work force; unlike working people, they are thus unable to recoup their losses and bargain with their employers to offset inflation.
By assaulting those pensioners who border on the poverty line but, because of supplementary incomes, do not qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Government is effectively punishing those who were able or wise enough to practise the virtues of thrift and planning. That is not to denigrate senior citizens who are compelled to rely exclusively on OAS and GIS; rather, I am arguing for some consideration toward those who, through their own devices, are now being penalized for living just above the poverty line.
There is a further inequity in Bill C-131, as there is in Bills C-132 and C-133. Single pensioners with incomes of $9,000 lose $290 in the next two years, but a family with two children on an income of $27,000 will lose less than $50 over the course of the much vaunted six and five program. A single elderly widow who has to live on $9,000 a year thus sacrifices six times as much as family with an income of $27,000 annually. This is not to say that the Government should squeeze the latter any more than it is already doing, but it should get its priorities in order. Bill C-131 perpetrates that sense of injustice.
Much has been made by the Government of the allegedly temporary nature of this Draconian measure. But if and when indexing is reintroduced in 1985, the computation for OAS will be on a lower base than it would have been had full indexing been adhered to over these two years. Therefore, pensioners are to suffer a permanent reduction in the amount of OAS benefit. Unlike the public servants who were nailed under Bill C-133, these senior citizens cannot return to the bargaining table to make up that amount. In short, Mr. Speaker, the gamesmanship of six and five simply cannot justify the economic hardship that Bill C-131 will wreak among the elderly.

February 3, 1983
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
I want to mention again the door-to-door canvassing of my constituency which i undertook last September. Pensioner after pensioner expressed fear of continually rising prices, and said how even a cutback of $12 monthly would make a significant difference in coping with the grim realities of day-to-day life. Rents, food and the cost of everything that pensioners buy, go up. I do not think it is right for a Government that spends $100 million on advertising its own Departments to expect pensioners to bear the burden of the ever-rising deficit. Fully 62.5 per cent of my constituents who responded to a questionnaire believed that benefits to the elderly should be increased rather than decreased. The very people this Bill is now victimizing are the survivors of the great depression and two world wars; surely it is time that their struggle ended.
Another point which I wish to make is that this unjust and immoral measure will effectively bring few returns to the Government, for all the fuss it is making. Estimates from the Department of National Flealth and Welfare show that capping OAS will save about $31 million in 1983. Mr. Speaker, what is that against a projected budget deficit of $23 billion for this year? Let us look at other areas where we can cut Government waste; for instance, the Government will spend three times more on advertising its programs this year than it will save by putting the burden of inflation on the backs of the elderly of this country.
In addition, Bill C-131 really reflects a lack of confidence on the part of the Government in its own six and five program. If inflation truly does drop to the targets of 6 and 5 per cent, then this Bill will be totally unnecessary as OAS benefits will be indexed to these levels in any event. But if inflation is really substantial, then Bill C-131 is a monstrosity, for it will take income away from senior citizens right when they need it most. If the Government is so optimistic that it has the answers to the problem of inflation, then why does it want a Bill to do what its six and five program is touted to do?
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I am appalled at the Government's use of closure and what I expect to be its automatic rejection of the amendment offered by the Hon. Member for Calgary West. The Bill breaks trust, it creates hardship and it is an ad hoc response to a fundamental issue facing our society. We should have spent the time we have given to this debate discussing instead a program that the Government could bring forth to deal with the "greying" of Canada. Surely it is evident that in future a greater proportion of our population will be over the age of 65. This will present a great social problem and a challenge, as it will be necessary to change many aspects of our society. We must not only deal with the elderly but we must draw on their experience for the benefit of the whole of society, not treat them as cast-offs waiting to draw their last breath.
I shall present a motion on a comprehensive program for aging under Private Members' Motions when the new session of Parliament begins-if that ever comes about. This session seems to be going on interminably and is doing damage to Canada.
I want to address the crucial question of a comprehensive program for aging because I believe we are going to have to pay some very serious attention to ways of increasing the number of residences for senior citizens. We must also make more home support available to senior citizens. They want nothing more than to be able to stay in the homes they have had for years and have probably paid for. They may not need a great amount of money to live on but do need some support in the years left to them.
I should also like to see more support for cultural activities for senior citizens, and I should like them to have the opportunity to engage in voluntary and community work. There is an enrichment of society there upon which all of us can draw. It is wrong to think that because someone is over 65 they cannot make a contribution to society.
1 could talk for a long time about the number of famous people in history such as Schweitzer, Churchill, Pope John XXIII and any number of composers and artists who made great contributions in their fields and to humanity after they reached the age of 65. There will be an opportunity for more of that in the future because of the greying of our society. We do not want just to tolerate senior citizens or treat them as whipping boys. We must treat senior citizens as an integral part of society, recognizing in this new technological age that they can make greater contributions to our society if only we treat them decently and provide them with the basic level of support and services that they need.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand and oppose Bill C-131, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act. Once again, with obvious predictability, this Government has chosen to invoke closure with respect to a debate over an issue which is in strong dispute. Repeatedly, and with good reason, this Government has been described as arrogant. The word "arrogant" as we all know, means overbearing, presumptuous and haughty. The arrogance of this Government is reflected in almost every move it makes, every pronouncement it utters and every attitude it conveys. Now, its disdain for our senior citizens is shown by allowing only 17 hours of debate on this most important Bill and only four sessions to hear witnesses.
Nowhere and under no circumstances does this arrogance assume more dangerous proportions than when it seems to achieve a dismissal of the established democratic rights of this House, and by natural extension the rights of Canadians, whom we all represent, particularly, of course, our senior
February 3, 1983

citizens. This Bill abrogates a responsibility to those seniors who have an unwritten contract, as the Minister herself stated. The only factor in the whole pension scheme, in my view, which bears scrutiny is the universality aspect relating to the top echelon of the income scale.
What are the savings in this Bill? Perhaps some $30 million. I would like to take a minute to examine some of the waste of this Government and put it in perspective with regard to what it is willing to do to the seniors in the name of saving. How much did we waste in Haiti to pay left-wing dictatorships and their lackeys? Some $25 million. How much did we waste on the Unity Office? Perhaps $50 million. Then there was the advertising of the Constitution; loans to left-wing nations. Michael Manley got a $90-million loan, $10 million of it forgivable. Will we ever recover it? What about loans to leftwing nations at no interest or very little interest over terms of 20 to 50 years in the amount of hundreds of millions of dollars?
On the metric office, it spent perhaps $25 million. We have losing Crown corporations, dozens of them. According to the Auditor General's Report, most of them are absolutely and totally unaudited, operating on their own under the cloak of Government. Canadair alone owes this Government $1.5 billion. What is the tab for enforced bilingualism? It is $441 million. Their answer is to penalize the senior citizens of this great Canada of ours.
To invoke closure of debate on this Bill is to say to Members of this House and to their constituents that the Government has no interest in or regard for the opinions and needs of others. By invoking closure the Government is saying to us, to all Canadians, that what we want and what we feel is necessary in our lives is of no importance whatsoever.
By invoking closure the Government is saying: "We will decide what is best for you. We will make these important decisions for you. We are not interested in what you think, even if we waste millions of dollars on programs which are distasteful"-ones which my constituents do not want. By invoking closure, the Government is once again replacing democracy with dictatorship, a situation which I have spoken about in this House before and a situation which I regard with anger and distaste. I submit my outrage is justified, as is that of many Canadians who support that position.
Prior to this particular invocation of closure, there have been 14 times during this session of Parliament when this Government limited debate on issues before this House. As my colleague just mentioned, thank Heaven when it is over. On 12 occasions the Government has imposed time allocation, which we are now under, which is just a fancy word for closure; and on two others it resorted to outright closure in its true meaning. These were 14 actual instances when the Government was successful in imposing its dictatorial will.
There were other times when the Government attempted to invoke closure and was blocked, most recently when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) sought to whisk his controversial and disastrous Canagrex Bill through the House. The Hon. Member to my right presented a petition on behalf of his constituents only yesterday decrying this injustice. What
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
will Canagrex do? It will give the Government the power to buy and sell all agricultural products in Canada. The word for that, which I learned in my reading of Marx, is communiza-tion. It will cost more millions with another Crown corporation in place.
By invoking closure, the Government quite clearly reveals its lack of regard and respect for the Members of this House and, I repeat, for the people we represent, particularly our seniors. I might add briefly that this disrespect and disregard is further amplified by the Government's use of Orders in Council. This Government, much to its dismay, must present certain items of legislation to Parliament for examination, scrutiny and debate. That is our role on this side of the House, for the time being.
This Government, much to its dismay again, obviously finds the process of scrutiny distasteful. To have its destructive policies and its shallow reasoning subject to public scrutiny is an obvious irritant to this Government. It is much more simple and less embarrassing for this Government to pass Orders in Council whenever possible. How simple and, as I stated at the beginning, how arrogant! This arrogance is supported by fact. Since this Government was returned to office in 1980, it has passed a total of 11,345 Orders in Council, some 4,062 in 1982 alone.
What has been created by this by-passing of Parliament? A total loss of credibility, a total loss of confidence, people not knowing whether they can trust their banks or trust companies; and now contracts with senior citizens are broken. What it amounts to is a pox on the house of our senior citizens, particularly older women, many of whom have been on the low-wage scale all their lives or have received no wages whatsoever. We all know what the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) thinks of the spousal allowance and women volunteers. As my colleague who spoke before me mentioned, women have a great role to play in the voluntary sector of the country, particularly senior citizens.
Let us look at this Order in Council nonsense. There is VIA Rail, the beginning of the end of passenger rail service in this country. How many senior citizens wrote to me about the cancellation of the commuter train in the riding of Simcoe South? Literally dozens. It was their only mode of transportation to and from the city of Toronto.
The emergency planning order, arbitrary and far-reaching powers for a Government in a nebulous or manufactured emergency, included provisions, if anyone in this country could believe it, for the creation of civilian internment camps. I hope that right-wing senior citizens are not the first on the list.
There has been an increase in the cost of our postal service, another item that is very inflationary. It causes the seniors undue hardship. There has been no regard for a corresponding improvement in the postal service. There has been the imposition of mandatory metric weights and measures, costly and controversial to say the least. I am proud to join 36 other Members on this side of the House in the opening of a service station to give people that freedom of choice. The issue is not metric; the issue is freedom of choice. The issue is no Orders in Council.

February 3, 1983
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Orders in Council also provided for the pension benefits of Senator Pitfield and a handsome salary for the former Deputy Minister of Finance, lan Stewart-1 wish he spelled his name differently-while he looks for a new job.
What about the $200,000 to Ed Clark to languish on the Riviera while he becomes bilingual? He is one of the authors of the National Energy Program which is so disastrous to this country. What did he write his thesis on? If we are not talking about left-wing, then why was it on the Government of Tanzania? He is one of the people who is putting national energy programs in place for free enterprise Canadians.
Then there was the $70,000 to Mrs. Susan Warner in the Barrie office of Health and Welfare for language training in Toronto. Certainly that is required! They would not get one telephone call in French in a month. Waste, waste. Spend, spend. And now at whose expense? At the expense of our seniors who, the Minister admits, have a social contract with her Government. Most particularly it is at the expense of pensioners, who cannot recover lost income. They are in a fixed position, but they have to pay increases in costs for food, clothing and accommodation.
When this Government is ashamed of something it does, it does it secretly without reference to Parliament or to the people particularly, the over one million pensioners. When the Government has to go public, it uses every means available to limit and minimize debate and scrutiny. 1 am sure, Mr. Speaker, if it was at all possible, that this Government would have passed an Order in Council to limit senior citizens' pensions this year and next, and who knows when, if they could get away with it.
The ridiculous part of it is that none of this would have been necessary if pension funds in Canada had been put into a separate account, had been actuarially sound, had the Government backed them, and had free enterprise been allowed to invest in them. We would have had so much money in the pension accounts in Canada that we would not have had to lie to the people, to let them think there was a separate account, to let them think that they were forever safe from an encroachment on their pension. Bill C-133 also would not have been necessary in that case either. This act of Government is something it should be ashamed of and undoubtedly is the reason why, because it has to go public, it has now invoked closure on debate. I might add there are many more reasons why it would not have been necessary.
Why 14 years ago was this Government not looking at the economic crisis which was coming up? Why was it that Germany and Japan foresaw what was going to happen and really did something about it in their economic planning, in their research and development programs? Canada is now ranked 24th of 24 by the OECD in terms of economic growth, and I quote:
The OECD estimates that in 1982 the countries listed below economically grew at a faster rate than Canada.
The OECD goes on to list the countries. So we cannot blame it on the anchovies of Peru, or the penguins of the Antarctic, or the foxes of somewhere else, or on Mr. Reagan, because the countries listed are countries such as Belgium, Finland, Greece, Iceland, Luxembourg, The Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Turkey. We are behind those countries. We are 24th out of 24 and I do not think you can blame that on world inflation.
Of the OECD's top seven countries, Canada ranks second in the unemployment rate, second only to the United Kingdom by half a percentage point. We all know what happened to the United Kingdom the minute it embraced socialism: it has gone downhill ever since. We are falling into the same trap because of the Government across the way, which believes it is much easier to start any kind of uphill fight on the backs of our pensioners. Canada is the only OECD country of the top ten in which industrial productivity has decreased. Who are we going to blame that on?

speechtext: Do you know why?

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I know why-because of 14 years of totally inept Government planning. If we were putting the money in R and D, everyone knows what it would do; even one-half of 1 per cent would provide some 400,000 jobs. Everyone knows the success of the Mitels of this world. But what do we do? We throw money at all kinds of make-work projects which will do nothing but further increase inflation and, for heaven sakes, we put it on the backs of the pensioners!
Perhaps it might be appropriate at this time to underscore and identify more clearly the nature of the shame involved, as the Hon. Member just said. The Minister of National Health and Welfare when speaking to the House on the Bill before us said she was doing the senior citizens a favour by arbitrarily enlisting them in the Government's sloppy battle against inflation. Some favour! It is like saying to someone who has just been the victim of a pickpocket: "Well, now at least your pants won't bag"; or telling the victim of a purse snatcher that a weight has been taken off her shoulder. Such reasoning defies logic. Such reasoning defies credibility when we are only saving $31 million, with a deficit like we have. Yet such reasoning is absolutely and totally typical of this Government. To offer such shameful reasoning to a particularly important segment of our society, believe me, Mr. Speaker, is without precedent.
The importance of our senior citizens, our deep regard for what they have done and continue to do, is perhaps the basic reason I find this Bill so shameful. Senior citizens are not old age people; they are Canadians over a certain age who have a lot more to contribute. I do not think we should forget the quotation; "Honour thy father and thy mother, that their days may be long". That is something this Government should take a long, hard look at, especially now when they are taxing somebody extra for being over 65. Canada did not spring full blown from the forehead of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), much as he would like to take credit for that creation, too. How do you suppose our senior citizens feel now
February 3, 1983

about the Charter of Human Rights? How much confidence do they have now in the people across the way?
Canada grew, developed and prospered over the past 116 years solely through the efforts of its citizens. Many of those citizens who hewed, harrowed, hallowed and clawed their way through the depression years know what the real cost and sacrifice is of being a Canadian. They have never complained, so why should we hit them first? Canadian citizens in every walk of life work hard and with diligence to create a better environment for themselves and for future generations. Those contributions were made in the home, in the marketplace and on many occasions on the field of battle, and I know we are all proud of the distinction with which they served in preserving the right of freedom which we stand in this House and champion.
Each new generation, understanding and appreciating these efforts, applied themselves with equal enthusiasm and sense of purpose, but this is being eroded by this Bill. The growth of our nation and our advancement as a society has been the result of all that hard work and diligence. Our acknowledgement, gratitude and respect for such services from our seniors should be without question. There should be no doubt of our ability to assume the continuing task without asking those who have given so much to give yet more, or to be hurt in any way. Yet through this Bill, the Government is doing just that, except with respect to the top scale of those receiving the old age pension. This year and next, and knowing this Government likely in the years to follow, the very pension we offer our senior citizens could well be reduced again by the simple means of an Order in Council, or by bringing some measure in and attaching closure to it.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has said that it would only be a 50-cent reduction. Fifty cents more for the Government to waste with its profligate spending. Fifty cents to give away to anyone, but not to our senior citizens, one of our most important commodities. Fifty cents! Is that not marvellous? The Minister is telling us that this stupid act of disrespect is for 50 cents. For shame!

Madam Speaker, since the first of February, American and Honduran forces have been holding large-scale joint military manoeuvres in Honduras, less than 20 kilometers from the Nicaraguan border. This military exercise, called Big Pine, is the largest one ever organized in Honduras by the U.S. army. These manoeuvres are being held at a time when relations between the U.S. and Nicaraguan governments are particularly tense, and their aim is to intimidate and destabilize the Sandinist regime.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, recent demonstrations by Canadians show three citizen concerns-the build-up of arms and instruments of mass destruction, unemployment, and support for the world's oppressed. In view of these anxieties, why does the effective role played by Canada in the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe receive so little attention by Canada's media when that Conference holds possibility of progress in all three of these areas-in easing international tensions through dialogue and negotiation of confidence-building measures, in producing new employment by reducing barriers to trade, and in progress in human rights leading to freedom from oppression for such people as Anatoly Shcharansky, whose hunger strike has so possessed the souls of Canadians? EFFECT OF NEW POLICY ON WESTERN FEED GRAINS- ANXIETIES OF QUEBEC FARMERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on Tuesday the Canadian Government announced a new western grain transportation policy. It seems that the announcement has raised a number of questions among Quebec farmers regarding the survival of the agro-food industry in that province. I would like to take this opportunity to recall that the policy statement includes a number of measures aimed at ensuring that there will be no adverse effects for agriculture in Quebec. First of all, there will be a four- and not a seven-year plan; the Livestock Feed Board of Canada is to set up a mechanism to monitor the effects of this transportation policy; and a task force will be set up to determine a fair and non-discriminatory payment system for Eastern Canada. There is also the assurance that the price of grain in Eastern Canada will not be affected by the new policy; that Quebec's diversity of supply will be maintained; that any additional payments to western producers will require the passage of legislation; and that a study will be carried out by the railways in Eastern Canada to explore ways of improving transportation for agricultural products from Eastern Canada.
Therefore, claims that the Government of Canada will be spending $3 billion on developing agriculture in the West are just not true. I may remind the House that the purpose of this policy is not to improve agriculture but to improve the transportation of agricultural products in Western Canada.

CALL FOR INCREASED UTILIZATION OF PORT OF CHURCHILL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the present time several Ministers of the Crown are in various parts of Canada holding news conferences and meetings, publicizing planned changes in the Crow rate and the expenditure of several billions of dollars to modernize the railway transport system.
The Port of Churchill is an integral part of our transportation system, yet the Government has totally ignored it in its proposals. The Port has never been used to capacity and has a potential which has never been exploited. With the new proposed freight rate structure, the cost savings of using Churchill will be much more substantial than they are now. Increased capacity and utilization would greatly assist in movement of the projected 30 million plus tonnes of export grain, and relieve some of the bottlenecks in the system. As well, it would mean lower costs for goods imported to western Canada from Europe.
While I realize there are certain problems because of permafrost and ice, I suggest that these problems are not insurmountable. Techniques involved in constructing the Alaska Gas Pipeline, and reinforced hulls developed for Arctic shipping, should be considered.
If the Government is serious about modernizing our transportation system and developing industry in the West, I would suggest that it spend some of its funds now for Churchill.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the New Democratic Party supports the development, modernization and expansion of railways for the benefit of all Canadians. The New Democratic Party recognizes the direct effect on the economy which such expenditure will have through jobs in the steel industry and railroad communities across Canada.
Western grain producers will appreciate the possible effects that such upgrading of railways will have on the movement of grain. This upgrading process is long overdue and has been neglected by the railways and the Government. In fact the movement has been the other way-to downgrade and abandon rather than to improve.
February 3, 1983

The New Democratic Party welcomes this change in Government policy and hopes that the Government has enough business sense to ensure that the Canadian people will gain equity in the railways for the tax dollars spent.
The New Democratic Party does not agree with the removal of millions of dollars of income from western grain farmers by changing the freight rate, the Crow rate, which farmers have to pay. For every dollar that a farmer earns, there is a multiplier effect of $6 or $7 across the country. A billion dollars, which farmers will have to spend on freight, will amount to $7 billion being diverted from the machinery industry, the fertilizer industry, the petro industry, the chemical industry, the food processing industry, and the retailing industry.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) has been questioned and pressed to make statements and give progress reports regarding matters dealing with veterans, yet he chooses to remain silent. The Minister says little, and does less, as though all were well and rosy within the Department. He has been asked about the length of time taken in processing veterans' pension applications, the aging veterans programs, Indian war veterans, Hong Kong veterans, War Veterans Allowance, compensation for prisoners of war, the implementation of recommendations by the United Veterans' Association and Committees, such as the Woods Committee and the Senate Committee on Health, Welfare and Science report entitled, "They Served, We Care". Still the minister does not inform us of the action he plans to take.
Just recently two of my colleagues questioned the Minister regarding ongoing problems veterans have been facing for years, yet we hear evasive answers, and no accomplishments are made. The Minister is contacted both in and outside the House and in Committee, in an attempt to have him reveal the developments in progress to better the conditions for veterans, but to no avail. These matters have been raised in the Senate, and still nothing is done.
The patience of my colleagues, of myself and, most important, of the veterans of Canada, is wearing thin. We want to know what the Minister is doing. We want to hear the plans he has made, the action he is taking, and we want the Minister to provide progress reports on his so-called investigations through motions in the House.

To assist them better, the reactivation of the 1935 Farmers'

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subtopic: DEMAND THAT GOVERNMENT DISCOURAGE USE OF LEADED GASOLINE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, research has shown that lead pollution of the air we breath is a very serious matter. This poison could retard the brain development of thousands of Canadian children. Over the last few years we have been losing the war against this pollutant due to the attractiveness of low price leaded gasoline over unleaded gas.
The incredible increase in the price spread between leaded and unleaded gas is forcing budget-conscious consumers to substitute polluting leaded fuel even in vehicles built for the unleaded variety. In Ottawa, for example, the price spread has almost tripled in the last three years.
Today we learned that General Motors of Canada plans to reintroduce lead tolerant car to the marketplace in response to consumer demand and, according to Martin Rivers of Environment Canada, such a move would mean lead emission levels will "shoot right out the window."
I have brought this problem to the attention of the House and of the Government two or three times before. The Government knows that the increasing cost of unleaded gas is a result of tax policies and unacceptably high markups by oil companies so the companies can simultaneously increase profits and protect their investment in antiquated leaded gas refinery systems. The Government also knows that our lead emission standards are inferior to those in the U.S.
On behalf of the people of Canada I demand, that the Government stop enticing Canadians to defile our environment and use its taxation and regulatory powers to discourage a resurgence of leaded fuel use.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to see that the Government is taking steps, through proposed changes in labelling, to provide consumers with increased amounts of useful information on the nutritional value of foods sold in Canada.
The advantages of a uniform and standardized system of nutrition labelling are clear: consumers, particularly those with food allergies or needing to monitor their intake of substances, such as sodium or sugar, will be able to make better informed choices as to the best food value for their dollar. Manufacturers who wish to promote the nutritional value of a product will be required to substantiate such claims by providing relevant information on the label.
The Government is allowing a 12-month period for discussion of these proposals and has invited the co-operation and participation of industry and of consumers. Some manufacturers will be test marketing the new system later this year, which will allow some experience with it.
The proposals for nutrition labelling have great potential to benefit consumers and industry. 1 hope that Canadians will use this opportunity to become acquainted with the proposals and their implications, and to make their views known.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. It is related to the policy decision and the Crow rate announcement. There is no dispute anywhere in the country about the need to rebuild the railroads. I believe everyone agrees on that. The dispute centres around how the rebuilding should be funded.
Given that the farmers have been facing a particularly difficult financial squeeze for a number of years and that to impose an additional cost on the farmers today could result in only one of two things, a reduction in their cash flow or an increase to the consumer, which quite frankly is not able to occur under the structures in place, would it not make more sense to ask CP to invest a substantial sum from the very large profits it has been able to derive from its operations in Canada, together with an equal investment from the Government, the people of Canada, in building a railroad system that will satisfy the needs of the country as a whole, rather than to put the cash flow and the very existence of our farmers in jeopardy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the reality is that the Government of Canada, that is to say, the taxpayers of Canada, have been and would continue for several years to pay hundreds of millions of dollars to the
Oral Questions
railways in order that they continue operating in the West because they were transporting merchandise at rates set historically at levels which did not permit the railways to operate. Therefore, there had to be some change in order to permit the Government of Canada not to continue subsidizing the CPR and the CNR ad infinitum for one, two, or three more decades, to the tune of many, many billions of dollars. Something had to be done in order to stop that.
What was done was not, as suggested, to make the farmer pay more this year or next year. That is not the solution proposed. The solution is that the farmer continue to receive what he has been receiving historically, but in terms of increased cost in terms of inflation that he be asked to share, as every other Canadian is asked to share, in meeting these increased costs.
That is the proposal that the Government put forward. It seems not only eminently fair to me, but it seemed in principle eminently fair to Mr. Gilson who made the survey, heard all parties, and arrived at a general recommendation along those lines. It is easy for the NDP to say that the Government should pour many more hundreds of millions and billions of dollars into the railways. Somebody has to pay for it. In terms of increased cost it does not seem unreasonable that the farmer be asked to share along with other Canadians in the payment of those increased costs.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member who had just finished his remarks prior to our seeing the clock at one o'clock; I believe it was the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart). In the Hon. Member's speech, he referred favourably to the economies of Germany and Japan and did what a number of his colleagues are in the habit of doing, that is, holding up Germany and Japan as countries which Canada ought to imitate. In the same speech, the Hon. Member also waxed on uncritically about the virtues of free enterprise and non-intervention of the Government in the economy.
My question is in the way of a comment to the Hon. Member. When is the Hon. Member, and others like him, going to show some theoretical consistency? When are they going to grow up and admit that the economies which they hold up as worthy of imitation are economies in which there is a long standing tradition of Government intervention in the economy, Government planning of the economy, the very kinds of things which, when they are attempted in this country, the Hon. Member gets up and denounces as the horrors of socialism? When is he going to show some kind of consistency? If he is not going to do that, would he spare us these speeches which make absolutely no sense at all?

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard these diatribes from the socialists to our left before. What I am talking about is the fact that those economies have invested money in the proper areas, not wasted it as do the Government on North-South dialogue and diatribe. Those economies have produced the money by the free enterprise system, not by state control which every one of the NDP advocate. Why don't they stand up some time in the House of Commons and say: "We advocate state control"?
