speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this Bill this afternoon. I believe Bill C-131 is the topic we are supposed to be on; the short debate we had previously was enjoyable, but it did not make too much sense to me. There were some points on the extreme left that were raised but they were not relevant to the Bill we are debating.
This Bill, Mr. Speaker, limits the increase to the old age pension plan to a maximum of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. Old Age Security now sits at $246.62 a month and should increase to $271.61 on January 1, 1984, but will only increase to $261.74. That is a difference of $118.50 a year. This legislation is directed at the 1.2 million senior citizens who do not qualify for full or partial Guaranteed Income Supplement. Assuming that inflation stays at its current rate of 10 per cent, each one of those 1.2 million senior citizens will lose $290 in the next two years, or just over $70 next year and a further $220 in 1984.
Some of these people are single, elderly people with incomes just over $8,900 per year. That is the cut-off point for those who receive the full Guaranteed Income Supplement. Those receiving more than $8,900 a year, whose incomes are just in excess of that figure, are the ones this legislation hits hardest. If they live in urban centres such as Quebec City, Montreal or Toronto they already live below the poverty line.
The married elderly with incomes just over $15,000 per year will suffer a loss in income over the next two years of $580. We are talking about 50,000 elderly people-25,000 single and 25,000 seniors living as married couples with incomes between $15,000 and $16,000-who will be hardest hit by the Government's six and five legislation. It appears that the sum of money the Government hopes to save from these 50,000 senior citizens will hardly make a difference to this Government, which is the biggest spender of all times. But this $15 million or $20 million does make a difference to the 50,000 senior citizens. The $12 per month that it represents can make a big difference.
The number in Canada of those 65 years and over has risen to more than 600,000 in the last ten years alone. That age group is growing at an annual rate of 3 per cent. This means that without any increase in real benefits the economy will have to grow 3 per cent each year to provide the necessary revenue to support the pensions of these people. Also it means that the larger the population reaching age 65 with little or no
February 3, 1983

Canada Pension Plan or private savings, the greater the public burden will be since these people will have to be supported by the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
The population from infancy to age 17, on whose behalf Family Allowances and the Child Tax Credit are paid, is declining. There are about 850,000 fewer people in that age group today than there were ten years ago. This means that Family Allowances and the Child Tax Credit will be less of a burden on the public over the next few years than in the past. Also it means that an increased portion of the population is of working age and is contributing to the economy. Therefore, we could adequately support those who will be retiring within the next two decades if we were to use this period wisely.
The Bill attempts to bail out the Government from its own economic and fiscal mismanagement and place the burden on the backs of the elderly. Most Canadians are willing to share the burden of reducing inflation. Most Canadians are able to reduce their lifestyles to their incomes. Old age pensioners are being told that they will have to cut their already small pensions to conform to the six and five policy of restraint. Although the six and five program is a small step in the right direction, it should have considered the exemption of Old Age Security recipients, as many senior citizens have a hard enough time without having to cope with decreases in their pensions.
A 10 per cent inflation rate in the country, coupled with a 6 per cent decrease in pensions, will have a devastating effect upon seniors who are now only able to cover the costs of the bare essentials of life. Restraint should not be imposed upon those citizens who can least afford it. It is not fair to ride out the recession on the backs of our senior citizens by seeking restraint from those who can ill afford it. Approximately 20 per cent or 600,000 of our elderly live in poverty. We also know that senior citizens are forming an ever-increasing segment of our population. This is why we must take a serious look at all our pension needs to ensure that at the time of retirement one is able to live out one's declining years without worrying about having enough funds on which to live.
Pensions should be looked at as deferred income upon which we will draw once we leave the workplace. Also we must make sure that all pensions are not drained of funds by over-extending loans to the Provinces. There should be sufficient funds to ensure the presence of actual money, not just paper figures.
Because of the lifespan of people today, we must study the impact this will have on the national economy. Approximately 2,000 years ago the average life expectancy was only 22 years; 75 years ago in Canada the life expectancy for males was 48 years and for females 51 years. The average life expectancy today for males is 74 and for females between 76 and 78 years. Today's 65-year-old man or woman probably has greater vigour, stamina and health than the 50-year old of the 1900s.
There is no question that the lifespan of man will continue to increase. We may be forced to review retirement practices in industry. We may find it desirable to lean toward the direction of voluntary retirement, depending upon the health of each worker. The human values of forced retirement at age 65 cannot be overlooked. Suddenly, at 65, a person who has spent
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
most of his or her life in the labour force is no longer allowed to contribute. He or she is suddenly cut off from his or her working companions, and just because he or she turns 65 is supposed to stop functioning. How can we justify this kind of treatment when today these very same people have been the most active senior citizens in the history of the country? A person who is forced to retire at the magical age of 65 is faced with more than a loss of income, and in many cases must learn to deal with emotional problems which are every bit as serious as economic ones.
When we consider the hardships which seniors experienced and lived through, such as two world wars and a devastating depression in the 1930s, we must re-examine the methods by which we express our thanks and gratitude. Senior citizens have already paid the price; we should not, by cutting back on their pensions, ask them to pay more.
People who are now aged 65 were born in 1917. They experienced a few good years after the First World War, and then came the depression. People who have not lived throught the Great Depression will never know what it was like, and our seniors who lived through it still suffer because of malnutrition and lack of basic essentials. They did what they could to make the best of the situation.
Then came World War II. All through these years Canadians co-operated. Many young men and women gave up the best years of their lives to do their part in the Canadian war effort. After the war they watched as the country underwent many changes, and still they co-operated. Today we are calling upon these people once more. We continue to burden them with the problems of the Canadian economy. We should realize that these people have already done their part many times over and that they should at least have the right to live as they see fit.
Today in Canada we need a drastic change of attitude. Not only do we have to realize what elderly people have accomplished, but we must also realize that we should not put our elderly people on the shelf. Many seniors are able to work and want to work, but modern methods of business and industry deny them the opportunity to do so. Older Canadian citizens have a treasury of skills and experience which can be used throughout our community. There are approximately 400,000 people in Canada receiving pensions, most of whom are women who fall below the poverty line. The approach of the Government in Bill C-131 does not deal with the problems facing us. The Canada Pension Plan will need contributions of around 9 per cent of earnings in the future instead of the present 3.6 per cent to maintain the present level of benefits. At the present time the Canada Pension Plan looks as if it will be bankrupt by the year 2020. It is discouraging Canadians from investing for their old age or retirement.
The high level of taxation and erratic interest rates are eating up the savings of senior citizens and are part of the economic mess which the Government created. The Government must try to correct the present economic situation, but not by the means proposed in Bill C-131. It will mean great

February 3, 1983
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
hardship for senior citizens and will reduce the savings of those who planned for their retirement.
Bill C-131 will attack those least able to absorb the six and five program and the group least able to influence changes on its behalf. The group is being asked to shoulder a burden which will have greater impact upon it than upon any other segment of Canadian society. The Government seems almost two-faced about its moral responsibilities and the narrow political motivations of its regional caucus. Statistics Canada indicate that the poverty line for single individuals living in metropolitan areas is $8,922, or $10 more than the Guaranteed Income Supplement. While it may be true that the GIS will be indexed to compensate for the limited indexation of the Old Age Security pension, the loss of any amount at all will be very difficult for the single pensioner whose income is about $9,000 or $10,000 per year, or the married couple with combined earnings of slightly over $15,000 per year.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said:
We are asking 1.1 million old age pensioners to help lead the way to fight inflation.
By this, the Minister is actually asking some 300,000 seniors, whose only form of support is the Old Age Security pension, if they will volunteer to be in the front line of restraint. These are the people who survived the hungry thirties, served the country in wartime and built up our industries in the post-war era. I can safely say that if the Minister was actually to ask senior citizens at random if they support limited indexing, she would get quite different results than the ones expected by the Government in the House of Commons.
It is important that Canadian people, in general, take a look at how we treat our senior citizens. This is important because it says something about the way we look at human dignity and the value of people. In many cultures older citizens are the ones who receive the greatest respect. They are the ones the rest of society looks after in a very special way. The senior citizens, the wisdom of the community, are held together and looked after and cared for by the whole community. For centuries the Chinese have respected the wisdom of the old, and this is true in their culture even today.
I represent the riding of Malpeque, Prince Edward Island. P.E.I. has a unique situation. There are probably proportionately more elderly people there than in many of the other Provinces of Canada. In the riding of Malpeque alone we have 3,325 senior citizens out of a total population of 32,628, according to the 1981 census. When I speak on this Bill, therefore, I speak as the representative of many people who will be affected by the cutback in their pension and the fact that their pension will not keep up with the cost of living.
These people, having lived in the Maritime region in Canada, know only too well the sacrifices that have to be made as a result of rising costs. A great portion of these people have spent their lives doing physical labour, working the land or fishing. Some of these people had to move to other parts of
Canada in order to find job opportunities. But as many Mari-timers do, they returned home a few years later wishing to spend their remaining years in the peacefulness of their own Province with a sense of security and belonging. Now this Government plans to take away this small sense of security. The worry of finances has always been a problem for these people, and the six and five program continues to create hardships for them, even in their old age. These people do not live in metropolitan centres but in a high-cost region. Yet the Government insists on taking from the poor and defenceless.
Our Canadian seniors did not have unemployment insurance as a safety measure when they were out of work. They could not depend on social assistance and welfare to help them when they were unemployed. Anyone who speaks to senior citizens can read the hardship in their eyes as they tell of their experiences with poverty. I cannot imagine any government attacking the people who built this country and made it what it is today so that we all can prosper. We are saying to them, "You have to sacrifice some more. You have not sacrificed enough". Yet these elderly people have had their lives shortened because of the privation they had suffered and the struggles they had when they were young.
I feel that Bill C-131, if passed, would further demonstrate this Government's lack of concern for the Canadian people and demonstrate how unjustly it treats our citizens. This Government is attacking the weak who cannot stand up to its wrath.

Mr. Speaker, I will be brief but I felt compelled to speak to the House primarily because of the anxiety, concern and fear of many of my constituents and friends who fall in the category of senior citizens. Talking to them, reading their letters, wining and dining with them, if you like, I have found that maybe 90 per cent of their concerns are based on misconceptions of the legislation before us. This, I think, reflects on me, on other Hon. Members of the House and particularly on our Party, since it is our legislation. We are not consciously reminding our senior citizens about the intent of the Bill and what it is designed to do. It is designed not to destroy old age pensions but, on the contrary, to protect the basic principle of what has to be considered, I think, as one of the most enlightened, progressive pension plans of any country in the industrialized world. It should be because, as the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) pointed out to us, our senior citizens in many, many instances, have been deprived of the possibility of earning a meaningful income with which to provide for themselves as a result of the depression, the war and recessions. As a general rule, it is safe to say that many of our senior citizens reach the age of 65 with very little in the way of investment income. I think it is imperative that this Party, in fact, all Parties in the House, remain as determined as ever to see that the basic principle of old age pensions stays intact.
Essentially, that is precisely what this Bill intends to do. I must confess my bias toward the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) who has shown great dedication to the problems of senior citizens and, to women, reflecting not only her natural compassion but her years with

February 3, 1983
the Commission on the Status of Women and her particular interest in social policy and social reform both in and out of the House. I was surprised at how many senior citizens fail to appreciate the fact that those senior citizens receiving the GIS are not in any way affected by this legislation. I think it might be useful to review for the senior citizens who may be listening and for all of us who are approaching that age, that all Canadians, by virtue of the fact that they are Canadians, regardless of their status in life, whether rich or poor, are entitled to a basic old age pension. We have never sullied that pension in recent years with the concept of a means test. We have said that all Canadians because of their contributions, so eloquently described by the Hon. Member for Malpeque, are entitled to a basic old age pension. We can, however, argue whether that old age pension is sufficient or insufficient. Periodically it has been improved. In respecting the new 20-minute rule, I will not trace the history of pensions, which were once applicable at age 70 and one day, we hope will be applicable at age 60. Regardless, the fundamental basis of our policy is that each and every Canadian is entitled to a pension, and there is nothing in this Bill which destroys that principle.
Years ago we recognized that in order to protect the sanctity of pensions, they had to be viable and economic, not threatened by the economic problems of our good friend, the United States, or the target of every right-wing person in the country. We recognized that there are many Canadians, who, for one reason or another, cannot live on a basic old age pension. They were in the work force probably before the Canada Pension Plan reached its maturity. Not through a means test but on the basis of income tax paid, we provided what is known as an income supplement, in other words, an addition to the basic plan. What the Minister has been able to do here by way of a compromise in the light of the problems we have at the moment is to suggest, in fact to guarantee, that any senior citizen obliged to request or obtain the GIS will continue to have that GIS and the basic old age pension fully indexed. That has not been explained sufficiently in the House. Because of the partisan nature of the House, speakers have glossed over this fundamental principle. As a result of glossing over this fundamental principle, they have created unfounded fears among many of our senior citizens who fail to understand the Bill, as many of us fail to understand the complicated measures.
I can reassure those people who receive the GIS that they will continue to receive it. It will continue to be fully indexed, as will their basic old age pensions.
Who is being asked to make some kind of sacrifice through a curtailment of some benefit through this Bill? It is those Canadians who are fortunate enough not to need the GIS. They are Canadians from all walks of life who, through good planning or good fortune, have other income over and above their old age pension. These Canadians are hardly envious of those receiving the GIS. They are glad they do not need it because it means more for other Canadians. We are simply asking those people to recognize the dilemma that this Government faced last year. Inflation was rampant in this country. It
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
threatened to run away, and the Government was forced to take action. The Government weighed the various alternatives at its disposal, from wage and price control to total disregard for inflation.
It is no secret that every economist in the world has a different view about how to control inflation. Even leading Nobel prize winners in the field of economics have opposing views on the question.
In its wisdom the Government suggested that we could not continue to shelter all Canadians fully by virtue of indexing. We were selective because of our Constitution as to who would make a sacrifice at a time when restraint was needed. They were Members of Parliament, Senators, public servants, members of Crown corporations and some senior citizens who had indicated in their tax returns that while they welcomed the old age pension, they did not need the GIS.
I often ask myself what would have happened to our pension plan if inflation continued to spiral to 20 per cent. What would have been the Government's position? I suppose it would have had to face the reality that the basic old age pension was insufficient. I hope the House would have insisted that the Government increase that old age pension. One would have to wonder how long Canadians who marry their private pensions to their old age pensions would have been able to survive. Certainly, people on fixed incomes suffer more than any other Canadian in times of inflation.
The thrust of the Government's plan was to bring down inflation and to allocate the sacrifice that was necessary in such a way as to enable us to maintain the sanctity of our concept of old age pension, in this case.
I do not wish to give an inflammatory, partisan speech because this subject is too important to drag into that type of environment. Fortunately, inflation has come down dramatically and continuously. When we capped the GIS and indexed salary increases, the level of inflation was at 11.2 per cent. At that time, limiting indexation represented a real sacrifice, if you like, of 4.7 per cent.
Today, as we are discussing this very Bill, the annual compounded rate of inflation since June is down to 7.2 per cent or, to round it off, if I am permitted, to 7 per cent. In reality, we are talking about a capping of 1 per cent or, to be specific, 1.2 per cent. As well, energy prices have come down throughout the world and other factors are bringing down inflation. I do not think anyone can accuse me of being a demagogue if I suggest that inflation could very well be at 6 per cent or less in this country by June. It really makes the exercise academic from that point on-

The Hon. Member, whom I never interrupt, laughs. I hope I am not pricking her sensitivities with clear logic. She may wish that inflation had risen to 20 per cent, but we do not. We think that it would have been disastrous for the country and for those living on fixed incomes. We believe it would have been a total disregard of the Government's responsibility to govern and bring down inflation in order to protect people on fixed incomes and to make certain that the Guaranteed Income Supplement and the concept of old age pension remain immune to attacks from those that would destroy it.
The Opposition likes to have the best of both worlds. They supported six and five. At least those Members in the corner did not support it. I suppose the temptation to address themselves to the fears of senior citizens was just too great for some Members. The fact still remains that those Canadians who must remain on a basic pension, and only the basic pension, have to make a little sacrifice.
The most difficult chore that a government is faced with in a democracy is to single out those who must pay or carry the burden of sacrifice in order to continue our democratic process. We have respected the need of those who unfortunately require the Guaranteed Income Supplement, and we will continue to index fully not only their GIS but their OAS as well. That group represents at least half of those Canadians who are collecting old age pensions.
I do not think I need to go on any further. I believe the figures with respect to the impact of indexing on the February cheques as opposed to the January cheques represent approximately 50 cents a month. If we all had our way, it would not even be that much, but as one who has prided himself on his concern for the senior citizen-I am sure all Members have this concern-we should be thankful that inflation has fallen to 7.2 per cent when capping is at 6 per cent. We should be thankful that the real impact on those who have to suffer the six and five implementation will be less. In reality, senior citizens are being asked to suffer the brunt of 1.2 per cent inflation, and not the original figure of last June which was over 11 per cent, therefore, rounded, almost 5 per cent.
I do not want to answer the hypothetical question, which I am sure should be asked, as to what we would have done had inflation continued at a rate of up to 15 per cent or 20 per cent. It is significant that it did not, and I am not even interested in attempting to claim that the six and five program was the main instrument in bringing it down, because then I would be partisan. My purpose in making this case today is really to respond to those senior citizens who have expressed to me, both by letter and in direct contact, their concerns, their worries and their uncertainties about what six and five means to them.
It means, fortunately, very little to those few people whom it will affect.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The Hon. Member is about to make his maiden speech.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
My colleague says that the Hon. Member for Kitchener is about to make his maiden speech, so perhaps we will hear from him on this subject.
The debate on Bill C-131, the Government's measure to limit the indexation of old age pensions, is unfortunately being brought to an abrupt and unnecessary end this afternoon by the imposition of closure. That is being done because the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) believes the debate has gone on too long. On this side of the House we believe that the debate should never have started. The spirit of the Bill is mean and petty. It is particularly miserly when you take into consideration that group of senior citizens whose incomes range just above the old age pension and GIS combined-people whose annual income is in the vicinity of $9,000 and $10,000. There are some 300,000 Canadians in that bracket and it is they who will feel the greatest impact from this Bill.
As well, the Bill achieves very little in the way of savings for the Government as it tries to combat the swollen and burgeoning deficit it has created. If we look at where we stood vis-a-vis inflation last year, we see that, as a result of this Bill, the Government will realize $10 or $15 million. That is a mere pittance compared to the Government's deficit spending this year which is upwards of $30 billion. That is for this year alone. But the Government reaches out to grab that $10 million from the senior citizens of the country at the same time as it continues its profligate spending on Government advertising, travel by Ministers and public servants or on fitting out offices. It is quite content to spend money in that way as it reaches out for the widows' mite.
The Government can argue that that is the way it is going to attain its objective of restraint, but at the same time it is handing out huge sums of money to bail out corporations that have got into trouble. How can the Government justify the fact that it is prepared to see $34 million go to Maislin Corporation, or half a billion dollars to Dome Petroleum while it claims it has to take $10 million away from the senior citizens of the country? Why should hand-outs to companies like this be right and proper while a senior citizen is asked to cut back a few dollars on his or her income? Those few extra dollars might make a difference to that senior citizen faced with the rising cost of living.
The eloquent Member for Lincoln said that a number of these senior citizens will have to practise a little sacrifice. Why should they have to practise a little sacrifice while the Government does not curtail its spending in other areas? That is why we on this side of the House cannot see any logic to the measure that is being pushed through this afternoon and, Mr. Speaker, neither can any senior citizen see any logic in this measure.
If the inflation rate continues at the 10 per cent rate it stood at last year, each senior citizen in the income bracket over and above $8,900 would stand to lose up to $300 in the next couple of years. That is what they would lose. That is a $300 penalty imposed on those who really cannot afford it, those who are not unionized or organized to argue their case and who depend on people here in the House of Commons to argue it for them. That is what I mean when I say that this Bill is mean and petty
February 3, 1983

in spirit. This Bill will not achieve very much for the Government, but it will penalize people in a way that is totally uncalled for.
I have said what they would lose if inflation were to continue at 10 per cent as it was last year. Suppose we take the optimistic scenario that the Hon. Member for Lincoln put forward this afternoon and the Minister of National Health and Welfare put forward at different times, that inflation comes down to 6 per cent and 5 per cent the following year or near it. Suppose we were to accept that scenario. One would have to ask what would be the use of this Bill at all because it does not save the Government any money. It does not do one single thing. All this does is to create anxiety, concern and uncertainty among hundreds of thousands of senior citizens all across this country. That is what it has been doing right along. The Hon. Member for Lincoln termed those anxieties and uncertainties "misconceptions". I have to tell him they are there. They are there because of the way in which this Bill was imposed.
I find it difficult to understand why it is necessary to proceed with this Bill. If the Government is out $10 million or $15 million, it can find that in savings in other ways. If inflation comes down, it gains absolutely nothing from this Bill and does not need to put it forward in the first place. Nothing that the Miniter or her colleague has said has convinced me or other Members of this side of the House that the Bill is necessary. Neither did they convince any of the organizations which appeared before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs when this Bill was in committee for study in detail.
I just want to list some of the organizations which appeared before us: The Canadian Council on Social Development, the Public Service Alliance of Canada, the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, the Economists and Sociologists and Statisticians Association and the Canadian Labour of Congress. All these organizations represented thousands of people who are staunchly opposed to the legislation.
The other day the Minister stated that there were no organizations which wanted to appear before the Committee when this Bill was being studied in detail. What she seemed unaware was that many organizations made their views about this Bill known when they appeared before the Committee on the complementary piece of legislation, Bill C-132, which is to limit the indexation of Family Allowances. I want to mention a couple of organizations which took that opportunity when they were appearing in committee on Bill C-132 to address themselves to the Bill we are debating this afternoon, Bill C-131. I mention two of them in particular because they represent the views of women. As is a known fact, the great majority of people of pensionable age, 60 per cent, are women.
The first group I want to refer to is the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women. That is the advisory Council to Government on the Status of Women. I want to quote what its President, Lucie Pepin, had to say at the committee hearings when the advisory council appeared on December 12,
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
1982. As reported at page 52:54 of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, she said:
-we are saying that in spite of the economic situation, which is very uncertain at this time, we would like the Government not to take any action in the area of family allowances and pensions. Not only do women make up the majority in these two groups, but, as several studies have shown, the poorest people in Canada are women. So obviously, that is what we are saying. We are asking the Government to be cautious because we do not agree with the action they wish to take. We feel that these two programs should not come under the six and five program.
That was the statement of the President of the Government's Advisory Council on the Status of Women. Did the Government listen to what was being said? It totally ignored the advice it was being given by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. That should not surprise any of us. On many occasions previously the Advisory Council or its President has spoken out. I think particularly of its former President, Doris Anderson. We know how completely ignored the advice put forth by the Advisory Council has been by the Government on critical issue after critical issue.
One of the other groups that appeared before the Committee was the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. That is the umbrella group which represents some 230 women's organizations across this country, some three million to four million women. They, too, had strong opposition to this Bill. I want to read what they had to say at page 51:10 of the report of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs when appearing before us on December 9 last, it reads:
-we want to emphasize that the companion Bill to this one, which would limit the indexing of the Old Age Pension, makes even less sense to us. The main losers in capping the indexation will not be the wealthiest elderly, because they would have paid back a good part of their increase in taxes. As a result those who will be most affected are the near-poor elderly whose income is just a little too high to entitle them to a Guaranteed Income Supplement for the elderly poor.
We, therefore, call on all Members of Parliament-
She said all Members of Parliament, not just Opposition Members of Parliament.
-in the name of equity, as well as in the name of efficiency, to vote against both of these truly bad Bills.
That was the view of these two major organizations representing the women across this country, to vote against these two truly bad Bills. The Government has not taken that advice. I know it has not listened sympathetically to the views expressed by organizations, groups, individuals, senior citizens, Opposition Members, just about everyone has expressed opposition to this Bill, except Government Members. We are opposed to it because it is mean, petty, penalizes those who can least afford it, strikes out at women in particular and accomplishes very little except to exacerbate uncertainty, anxiety and concern among Canada's senior citizens.
I have received hundreds of letters and calls from across the country, on this issue. I talked to people in my constituency. I listened to what they had to say. I read their letters. I listened to those who came into my office.
I take calls from people who are truly upset because this Bill has created such uncertainty that they feel they do not know

February 3, 1983
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
where the Government will take action next or how it will next take action against them. 1 try to reassure them that their interests are being spoken to in the House of Commons, because a good many of us are trying to do that. But how can a person be really reassuring when the Government moves in, as it does this afternoon, with closure to put an end to debate on this Bill? How can you really reassure people that their interests are going to be protected when the Government lines up all its backbenchers and says, "Vote against it. Cut off debate. Don't let anything more be said on this issue." I hope that all senior citizen who are today represented by a Liberal Member of Parliament will take the opportunity to get in touch with that Liberal Member of Parliament and make it known very clearly how strongly they feel about the way their Member of Parliament has voted to impose this restraint on senior citizens, showing their responsibility for the difficulties which are being created by the Government.
It is very important, Mr. Speaker, that pensioners understand just why the Government is pushing this measure through. We all know that the economic situation in this country is in a terrible mess. Even the Government has to acknowledge that at this point. The Hon. Member for Kitchener says that it is not true that the country is in an economic mess.

Not true? I know that that is what the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Schroder) is saying, it is not true that it has been brought on by the Liberal Government. I am sure he is going to say that it is due to the international recession. Is that right? He nods his head. He says it is all due to the international recession. Well, I would like to ask him why it is that the recent OECD report which was published in December, 1982, shows that Canada's economic growth, its industrial development, ranks 24th out of 24 industrialized countries in the world? Why is it that, given all of those other international factors these other 23 countries had to absorb like Canada, they still do far better than we do? Can the Hon. Member tell me why we are at the bottom of the heap? Why is it that at this point we rank behind Italy, Portugal, Turkey, Iceland? Why is it we are at the bottom? It is because there is no responsibility here in this country for the economic policies which have been developed. That is exactly why we are 24th out of 24 industrialized countries. It is because the policies of this Government over the last two or three years have driven us into that position. And, as a result, what does the Government do? What does it do when it sees we are in this economic mess? It looks around the country and says, "Who are the people we can make the scapegoats?" When the Government
began to come to grips with this situation, as it has just begun to do, belatedly, who did it make the scapegoats for the things it has done wrong in the past? The first people it singles out are the senior citizens of this country.
That is what is wrong with this particular Bill. The Government is blaming its own failings on those who had nothing to do with it. I want to advise the Hon. Members opposite that they have their priorities totally wrong when they turn and point to the senior citizens of this country and say, "You are the ones who are responsible for the profligate spending. You are the ones who are responsible for the riotous living which has caused this economic mess." It is this Government which is responsible for the profligate spending. It is this Government which is responsible for the riotous living which has driven Canada into 24th place out of 24 industrialized countries. It is not the senior citizens of this country.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, we are so staunchly opposed to this Bill. We do not feel that the senior citizen should be asked to bear the burden of the Government's mistakes. That is why we feel, sir, that not only should this particular measure be given a six months' hoist this afternoon, but that this Bill should be lost forever.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the rhetoric of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I realize it is unfortunate to have to introduce facts into the situation for the Hon. Member, but I am going to do that and I will ask her to respond to such facts. We hear from the Opposition day in and day out, "Let's have some restraints. Let's reduce the deficit. Let's bring inflation down." Day in and day out they get up, and every time the Government introduces some form of restraint, the Opposition starts putting on its social conscience, something which has never manifested itself when the opposition was in Government because it has never introduced any major social programs.
The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands says our economic trouble is due to profligate Government spending. Let us look at the facts, Mr. Speaker. I will quote from the "Economic Review April 1982" put out by the Department of Finance of Canada, and we can compare total Government expenditures. If we look at this we will see that total expenditures of the central Government, the national Government, the Government of Canada, as compared to its GNP, between 1969 and 1972, was 14.0 per cent. In the United Kingdom it was 19.9 per cent; in the United States it was 18.0 per cent; in France it was 17.9 per cent. Let us move up to the middle of the decade. In Canada it was 16.8 per cent; in France, 18.3 per cent; in the United Kingdom, 24.0 per cent; in the United States, 19.6 per cent. All are greater than Canada. Let us move to 1979. In Canada, 15.6 per cent; in France, 18.2 per cent; in the United Kingdom, 24.6 per cent; in the United States, 18.2 per cent.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, the Government's spending on goods and services is not the cause of the increased deficit. The fact of the matter is we have had a
February 3, 1983

recession which has reduced revenues and increased expenditures in social programs because here in Canada, this Government has not taken an axe to the social programs as they have in the United States and in Great Britain, Conservative Governments which the Opposition has endorsed in the past.
I ask the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands why the Opposition continually hounds us that the deficit be brought down and, at the same time, whenever the Government introduces restraint in the transfer payments, or in any other area, the Opposition is up squawking? Put your money where your mouth is.

What it does do is to put a limit of six and five on indexation in general of Government expenditures through the six and five program. In addition, the six and five applies to indexation under the Income Tax Act. So that we are dealing with the problem of revenues indexed downward and expenditures indexed upward. Anyone with common sense will realize that is a deficit producing situation.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND

He keeps trying to say that if we are going to save money, we should be able to save it out of the cheques which go to senior citizens. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak against Bill C-131 because the principle involved in it is very important. It is the same principle which is involved in Bill C-132 and Bill C-133. The principle is that the Government has chosen to cut the spending power of certain groups, not the spending power of all people, as was quite erroneously, if not misleadingly, said by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary. There are certain important groups which the Government has refused to touch with its six and five program. In this case, in Bill C-131, it proposes to cut the spending power of about one million pensioners. Last summer the Government and the Tories basically agreed to this. The Tories would like the public to forget what they agreed to last summer, but I doubt that the public has forgotten or will forget.
The Government tries to cover itself, in the words of the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), by talking about the programs it introduced during more prosperous years in the past. He mentioned various programs. In fact, all of them were first proposed, and one of them first introduced, by the CCF and its Leader, not by the Liberal Government. It was the CCF, as led by James Woodsworth, who first put to the conscience of Parliament and this nation the necessity of providing social security. Although the CCF did not have the constitutional opportunity to introduce things such as Unemployment Insurance, it had and used the opportunity to introduce medicare. It pioneered medicare on the continent of North America. The claim of the Hon. Member for Lincoln is as hollow as most claims made on behalf of the Government.
Furthermore, now that inflation has been brought down by the international recession caused by the policies of this
February 3, 1983

Government and its allies in the United States and Great Britain, the Hon. Member is trying to claim that this Bill will not make any difference. The Hon. Member for Lincoln suggested that it would amount to only 50 cents-why bother spending all the hours spent by the Government preparing the Bill, all the dollars spent by the Government advertising its program and all the time necessary to debate this Bill, if all that is at stake is 50 cents? It is quite an incredible statement that the Hon. Member made. 1 do not think anyone could take him seriously. In fact, I think he is known as a man with a great sense of humour. I am sure he was speaking with his tongue in both cheeks.
My point is that the Government has chosen to cut certain classes of society and has gone against the principles about which it bragged, in the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), less than five years ago when he was taking a different tack than the one he is taking today. This was also at a time of inflation, in 1977, when he said:
In our society pensions provide a means of sharing risk so that we can retire in reasonable security and dignity without fear of the future. Protecting pensions from inflation by indexing them to increases in the cost of living should be an integral part of our pension schemes. Indexing does not give pensioners an increasingly larger claim on our economy's production-
This is in contrast to the groups the Government is now letting off scotfree. It does not give them a larger claim. He continued:
-that is, more money to buy things they could not earlier afford. Rather indexing merely enables pensioners to maintain roughly their same standard of living. Even a modest rate of inflation destroys at a devastating rate the buying power of people on fixed incomes. Pensioners are out of the workforce and cannot bargain or strike for larger incomes.
I would add that pensioners cannot raise the price of oil, interest rates in banks, the price of housing or the price of other goods on the market in order to obtain more income. They are the ones who are defenceless. They are not the cause of inflation. In any event, the Prime Minister said:
They are not the cause of inflation. They are its victim. We have an obligation to help protect them.
Well, that was almost five years ago. Clearly the Prime Minister has forgotten what he said then, but the people of Canada do not forget. By contrast it illustrates that the Government and the Tory Opposition, in complete agreement and totally in bed with each other on this point, will not cut the incomes of oil companies. The Government will not cut the excessive profits of banks and other lending institutions. It has refused to take any measure to restore the kind of control which was placed on banks by legislation for many decades until the 1960s. It will not even take any measure to acquire income tax from hundreds of Canadians who are earning more than $100,000 per year. These people not only are not cut, they are not taxed at all. The Government knows this well because it has reported on them. It refuses to take any action year after year to collect taxes from these people. Instead, it wishes to cut three classes of citizens. One is the pensioners. The second is the mothers of children. The third is public employees and some private employees. It is promoting the cutting of wages of all employees. We should notice that this is directed in a class sense against employees and completely
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
excludes employers. Employers are not to be cut by six and five. Employers are invited to cut their employees by six and five and, glory be, we have all kinds of patriotic employers who are willing to cut wages. So what is new?
In Spadina there are many pensioners. Many of them have telephoned and written to me to oppose this legislation. We have pensioners in the Senator Croll Apartments, at 250 Davenport, at 91 Augusta, in the Kensington Manor, in Central Park Lodge, in the Queen/John Streets Building, in Laughlen Lodge and at The Good Shepherd. Also there are many pensioners throughout the housing area of Spadina, people living in old houses. Many of them have paid for these houses over 10 to 40 years with hard work both in earning money with which to pay their mortgages and in maintaining their houses with their own labour. Now they are often living in these houses with relatives and maintaining them with careful savings. These people manage their money very carefully because they do not have much. Thanks to the Government they will have even less in real spending power.
Spadina is mainly populated by people who work to earn a living. There are a few self-employed people in Spadina, although very few of them are wealthy. Mainly the people of Spadina are construction workers, factory workers, building cleaning workers, almost all of whom are women, and domestic workers, almost all of whom are women. I mentioned factories but I especially want to mention the garment industry in which the great majority of workers are women, and the workers in small stores, in hundreds of restaurants, many of whom work 12 and 14-hour days, six, if not seven days a week, just to earn a very modest living. These are people who are often victimized by our economy even while they are employed. These people receive much less for their work than the people who get off scotfree from paying tax. The $100,000 and $500,000 types get off scotfree from paying tax. Instead of paying tax they would rather pay a lawyer, an accountant or a lobbyist with the Liberal or the Tory Party.
It is for the poor people who have already suffered that this Government is providing a cut in their pensions. The Government has decided to breach its contract. This Government, which is supposed to enforce the rule of law, as all Governments are, has decided to breach its contract, not only with its own civil service pensioners, but in a political sense to breach the kind of solemn contract which the present Prime Minister made years ago and reiterated five years ago in the words that I just read a few moments ago.
I want to quote a comment made by the Canadian Labour Congress. The Canadian Labour Congress is not speaking only for its own members, some of whom have adequate private pensions, adequate compared to what the majority of people in this country have, but it is speaking for all Canadians, including the poorest. It reads as follows:
Since 1964, OAS benefits have declined from approximately 20 per cent of average wages and salaries to approximately 14 per cent.

February 3, 1983
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
With average wages and salaries that could be considered to have roughly kept pace with prices-they have not, they have fallen behind-this means that old age pensions are two-thirds of what they used to be in buying power. These are the people whose buying power this Government now presumes to cut still further.
We have heard again and again and again, from the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), other Government Members and the Parliamentary Secretary, that this is such a small cut. We have heard them say, "Do not worry about it, it is only 50 cents," or whatever they like to say. But the question is why. Apart from the time spent debating this Bill, advertising it, and the clerical book work that is needed to make a change, I am quite sure that this costs more than the 50 cents. What is the Government's purpose? The saving clearly is not worth the aggravation that it causes to the individual pensioner. Nobody likes to have their buying power cut even if it is said the cut is not very great. Why make a cut if it will not bring in any serious revenue?
The Government's first appeal is to inflation. The Government says, "We have bad times. We have to do this to stop inflation." The Government has to cut payments to mothers, employees and pensioners to stop inflation while the Government allows the banks, the oil companies and the other large multinationals to run wild with their prices. That does not make any sense. A cut of the size the Government is talking about, as was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), does not do anything to stop inflation. It could easily be outdistanced by far by a saving in the Government's own advertising, in which it tried to misrepresent the six and five program to the Canadian people.
Why? This is a question the Government has never answered satisfactorily to anyone in this House or outside of the House. Therefore, I will suggest two reasons why this Government has chosen to single out and attack three classes of our society: employees, mothers of children, and pensioners, in this case especially the pensioners.
First, this is a neat way of undermining the principle of universality which the Government, along with the Tories, now wishes to do away with. What the Government has done is to reduce that part of the pension, a right that not only makes people rely more on that part of the pension which is subject to a means test but, in fact, it will force more pensioners from one group into another.
The Hon. Member for Lincoln talked about the people who are just on the margin. I was too far away but I thought perhaps I could see tears in his eyes when he was talking about these people who were just one dollar over the level at which they would get GIS. He is not here now. I am sure he has gone out to get himself another handkerchief with which to wipe his eyes. But the Bill which the Hon. Member for Lincoln is supporting, presumably, the Bill his Government has put forward and the Bill put forward by the Minister whom he says he admires so much, will take some of these pensioners, not on GIS, and force them to the level at which they will have
to apply for GIS. In other words, the Hon. Member will force more of the people of this country to rely on a non-universal type of pension. I think that is the intention of this Government. I think this is a small step, along with other steps this Government has taken, in such things as medicare, to destroy the very principle which the Hon. Member for Lincoln claimed to be supporting, the principle that there were certain allowances and programs that people have basically as a right. The Hon. Member for Lincoln claimed there was no change in the basic principle of a basic pension. Yet, he will be voting an hour from now to change that very thing, the principle of universality.
Since this Government will not give us a reason that makes any sense, we have to guess at it. I believe there is another reason why the Government is so eager to break its promise. On this point I will quote again from the Canadian Labour Congress which has, over the years, been a very good defender of pensioners and poor people, far beyond the ranks of its membership. This passage reads:
It clearly breaks a promise to Canada's current elderly, namely, the promise that the OAS program will provide benefits of a given real value. But not only does Bill C-131 break a promise to the current elderly, it raises doubts as to whether the arrangements that are now in place will be maintained for future generations of elderly Canadians. The fact that the Government of Canada feels free to reduce OAS benefits for reasons of short-term fiscal expendiency has the potential to breed a great deal of cynicism about the security of all future public pension benefits.
Another passage, referring to pensions, reads:
They should be treated as incomes to which people have earned rights-
I want to emphasize that point, Mr. Speaker. This is based on years and years of work by people who built Canada. These people have earned a right to a pension. This Government is now breaching its political promise to them. It is breaching a pledge that it made, again and again, so it could be re-elected. Writing about the pensions, this passage reads:
They should be treated as incomes to which people have earned rights based on the type of compact among generations mentioned above.
That is the position of the labour movement of Canada. It is the position of the Party I represent, and I wish we could fight the next election and the one after that on better issues than this. I wish the Government opposite and the Tories would agree not to trample on pensioners, on mothers with children and on employees as segregated from their employers. We still have to find this other reason. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has kindly given us the slogan. What she has said repeatedly here in this House and in committee is that the reason for this aggravating and senseless imposition on pensioners, employees and mothers with children, is to mobilize them. Her great slogan is "mobilize". During World War II, I and others joined the Forces because we were mobilized to fight an enemy. Others were mobilized to work in the factories and produce the means we needed to fight the enemy. However, no type of mobilization is being carried on through this Bill. Rather, it is immobilization. Rather, it is an attack on people's morale. Rather, it is an attempt to divide and set the pensioners against the workers, to divide and paralyze the
February 3, 1983

people of this country so that they will have no spirit to resist the actions of this Government and of the Tory Party, which would like to do the same and worse.
The mobilization argument is the phoniest argument 1 have ever heard, even from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). It is as phoney as a three-dollar bill. She does not want to mobilize people. She wants to immobilize and paralyze them and set them fighting against each other so as to weaken the fibre of this country. I am sorry that the Government has chosen a tactic like this which does nothing to stop inflation and will do great harm to the Canadian people.

Retired people in this country who have children and grandchildren who do not have jobs want jobs and a policy of job creation. They will accept 50 cents less a month from their pensions.

The test with respect to Bill C-131 is twofold. First, did the Government take an overview, and did it deal equitably and fairly with the senior citizens? It will be for the public to decide.
I think that this could be termed "the six bit debate", because that is exactly what it will cost a month, $1.50 or less a month if this Bill goes through. The Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) said, "It is a pittance", and those were her exact words. She then said that senior citizens are "anxious and concerned". I ask you, Mr. Speaker, who is causing this concern? The Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands said that when dealing with senior citizens who phone her, she tells them that the matter is being addressed. I would suggest that what she is telling them is, "Those Liberals down there do not know what they are doing and they are out to get you, but the Opposition will take care of your interests".

If she says here that it is a pittance, then she should tell them over the phone that this is a pittance Bill.
I have listened to the debate all day. One Hon. Member said that we have wasted $3 million on this debate, six days at half a million dollars a day. Another Member of the Official Opposition said that we have not debated the Bill long enough and that we should continue. I am listening and I want to learn. I have heard suggestions coming to me from the left, from the right and from the centre of the Party opposite, and I am no wiser for having been here the whole day.

What is the overview? First, there is world inflation, world unemployment and world recession. Second, there are record deficits. We had to borrow over $20 billion this year. Why must we borrow? It is because we want to keep social programs in place, and that is the only reason. It would have been just as easy to do what was done in Peru or Chile in an attempt to balance their budgets and continue their social programs.
The third part of the overview concerns the need for leadership. I do not think the six and five program is a panacea. I do not even suggest that it is a cure-all. However, it gives the direction which the public wants, even though the Opposition does not understand it.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
If we cannot control inflation and set a direction, what good are savings? In 1973, the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands returned from a visit to a country, Chile, where inflation was running at 1,000 per cent a year. As soon as people received their salaries, they went out and bought goods because the next day their money was virtually worthless.
If we cannot control inflation, what good is the saving? Second, what good is an industrial policy? That is only something on paper, and it will not work. I agree with the Hon. Members. The bottom line is a healthy economy, for if we do not have a healthy economy, we will not have all of the cultural benefits which the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) wants for senior citizens. We will not have pensions, unemployment insurance benefits or money. I therefore agree that we must have a healthy economy. If we cannot control inflation, we will not have a healthy economy.
Let us get rid of some of this rhetoric and set the record straight. What are we discussing? There are 2.34 million senior citizens in Canada. This Bill would affect 1.1 million and, in 1983, would mean that they would each receive 50 cents to $1.50 less a month. They will not suffer a decrease; rather, they will receive an increase. In December, 1982, a senior citizen received $249.92, and in January of this year will receive $250.62. Senior citizens will receive an increase. Do you want to know something, Mr. Speaker? They are happy. They know there is widespread unemployment. I receive calls from senior citizens along these lines: "You will cut $300 from my income next year". Where are senior citizens hearing this message? It comes from the Opposition. It is not true. They are getting an increase.
1 heard several Hon. Members today, and I will name them if I must, who spoke of the immorality of what we are doing. What is our record, Mr. Speaker? Since the days of Prime Minister Mackenzie King, through the Governments of Prime Minister St. Laurent and Prime Minister Pearson right to the present Prime Minister, all Liberal Governments have brought in measures of social change such as unemployment insurance, children's benefits, pension benefits and the Guaranteed Income Supplement. Major changes, from the Constitution to the trans-Canada pipeline and the St. Lawrence Seaway were Liberal policies and were usually strenuously opposed by the Panies opposite. This country is a world trader and sells $75 billion worth of goods per year to other countries. Is it immoral to say that we have to borrow $23 billion and so will have to take $1.50 of the pension next month but will still keep the $250. If that is immorality, then I should like to know what morality is.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said that the Opposition is playing political games. She is right, Mr. Speaker, and that is why this House is slowly becoming ineffective. That is why more and more decisions are being made by bureaucrats and Ministers. That is necessary

At least three speakers today, including the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) and the Hon. Member for Spadina, have said that fully indexed pensions are a social right. If they believe that, then they must believe that hospital care, education and any number of social services, are a right.

speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Then we come to this question. If the deficit is up, if recession is up, if the economy is down, if unemployment is up and if we have less revenue, then is it still a social right to be fully indexed?

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Yes.

If the answer had been no, then I would say that Hon. Members opposite do not fully understand Bill C-133. The key question is where we get the money. There are only three places we can get it-print it, impose more taxes, or borrow. I have not heard any of the more than 100 Members of both Parties on the other side that we should borrow more money, print more money or increase taxes.
I have heard those who represent the oil interests say that we should give more to the oil companies. I heard members of the same Party say that we should give more money to the North-South dialogue, and immediately after that heard another speaker say that we should give less to North-South. That is Party unity, Mr. Speaker. It is pushing and pulling at the same time. Those are the suggestions that were made today. The criterion is not what will work or what is best for the country but what will give the biggest headline in a member's constituency. That is not constructive debate and it does more damage to the credibility of the House of Commons than anything else we can do in the House. It shows a slow erosion that is almost irreversible.
I should like to return to the question of morality, Mr. Speaker. The test is whether things have improved in the last two or three generations. My grandparents did not have pensions or hospitalization or Unemployment Insurance. They lived on $30 per month. There were no benefits at all, no union protection and they only worked six months each year. Out of that $30 per month, $10 went for milk as they had eight or nine children whom they managed to support. But they had nothing at all. My parents had more, but they had nothing like as much as I do or as my children will have. I have legal aid, medicare and housing. They may have to go on a waiting list, to line up or wait their turn, but they are not deprived of housing. The housing program is fundamentally a Liberal program.
No Member of this House can say that things have not improved, Mr. Speaker. They must admit that there has been a giant leap in social justice in this country in only three generations. If that is immoral, then I do not know what morality is. If doing your job, trying to take reasonable
resources and spread them equitably is immoral, then I will get out of politics and go back to what I did before.

In Section 15-and I am going to be here to remind him of this for the rest of his life-there is a clause that says that no Government shall pass legislation that discriminates because of age. Yet today the Hon. Member tells us to vote against this Bill when he himself voted against Section 15 which would have disallowed discrimination because of age. He admits that he has done contradictory things in this House as he voted for six and five at one stage and will vote against it today. He has not done contradictory things just once, Mr. Speaker, but several times.
When I stand here later today I will vote on this Bill with the full knowledge that we all want to get to heaven, but some of us would like to get there with our socks on.

Mr. Speaker, there is one thing we can be sure of, that is, that we are not going to have another ten-minute question period.
I want to make a few observations with respect to Bill C-131, to state my support for the six-month hoist motion and, of course, to indicate my opposition in total to the Bill currently before us. That will be almost all the time I have to speak about it, but nevertheless I wanted to get those two points on the record.
The question asked is who will be affected by this Bill. The answer has been placed on the record quite often, so I will not spend too much time on it. Those who will be most severely affected by the Bill are those who have made the greatest contribution to the development and the building of this country. They spent years and years building, forgetful of their own needs, just barely able to get by. They were looking forward to the time, perhaps, when they could relax a little, when society would recognize and respect the contribution they had made and would assist them in their later years. There are those who, for various reasons, have been unable to provide security for their later years, some because of a lack of skills to compete in the labour market, others who have engaged in humanitarian services at low levels of income, and those who have worked in enterprises which have not provided pension benefits. There are others, including those over the age of 65, who are going to be particularly hard pressed because of this particular measure. 1 refer to the single persons over age 65 who do not receive any Guaranteed Income Supplement or spouse's allowance if their total income, including the basic old age pension, exceeds $8,900, a level of income $10 below the poverty line for single persons living in metropolitan areas. These are some of the individuals who are going to be affected by the provisions of this particular Bill.
The Government has said this Bill is not to save money, and it is set out in the questions and answers which came with the documents regarding Bill C-131. It reads:
The Government is asking all Canadians who have the means to lower their expectations over the next two years in order to help bring inflation down to 6 and 5 per cent. Some degree of sacrifice by all Canadians is required to bring about economic recovery in Canada.
When we consider this particular statement, Mr. Speaker, I think it points out the fact that it was meant mainly to take from those, reduce the income of those who could well afford it. But we all know very well, no matter in what area in the House we are sitting, that that does not apply to these people we have spoken of today because they have, for various reasons I have pointed out, not been able to make the savings which would enable them to invest and have returns, or in any other way provide for their later years. Therefore, the question now is, why is the Government proceeding with this particular measure? It has been emphasized today that inflation is down and it is not likely to rise for a while at least, and it may even go down below the 6 per cent or the 5 per cent, or whatever. That being the case, I believe this amendment is most appropriate, that is, to give this measure a six-month hoist in order that there might be an opportunity to gauge the effects of the downward trend of inflation, and then find out if it is really necessary, and if it is not necessary, then why in the world is the Government going to impose it on us? I make this plea because of the statements which have been made today by the Government spokesmen.
There is one more thought which I want to present, and that is the psychological factor. People who worked without any pension plan were fearful of the future. Canada Pension came in and new hope was born. Now, because of this particular measure, they are saying, "What next? What is the next Government step? Are we going to be reduced further?" So they are thrown again into insecurity, fear and uncertainty. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we are making an eminently reasonable proposal, that this be given a six-month hoist, and if not, then we certainly intend to vote against it and we trust that it will be defeated in the interests of those who will be so adversely affected.
